signals.title: CFP: Support dynamic IP address allocation in Cilium Network Driver
signals.text: ### Is your proposed feature related to a problem? The Cilium Network Driver proposed in [cilium/cilium#43295](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/43295) and [CFP-43295](https://github.com/cilium/design-cfps/pull/85) can allocate and prepare network devices for Pods through Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA). Those devices may also need IPv4 and/or IPv6 addresses, but the Network Driver does not have a scalable way to allocate them dynamically. Requiring a cluster operator to assign static addresses does not scale and is particularly unsafe with reusable `ResourceClaimTemplate` objects: multiple claims created from the same template must not receive the same address. Cilium Pod IPAM modes cannot be used directly because these addresses belong to claimed network resources, not to the Pod's primary Cilium interface, and their allocation lifecycle follows DRA prepare/unprepare operations rather than CNI endpoint creation and deletion. Without dedicated resource IPAM, operators must maintain per-workload address assignments themselves, cannot safely reuse claim templates, and cannot independently manage address capacity for different secondary networks or device classes. ### Describe the feature you'd like Add dedicated IPAM support for the Cilium Network Driver. It should manage addresses for DRA network resources and coexist with any IPAM mode used for Pods; enabling it must not change or consume capacity from Pod IPAM. ### Requirements - Support IPv4-only, IPv6-only, and dual-stack configurations. Allow cluster operators to define the address spaces available to DRA resources, including efficient use of small address ranges. - Support independently managed address spaces for different secondary networks or device classes, and allow each DRA device request to identify its intended address space. Cilium must not silently allocate an address from a different network when the requested address space is unavailable. - Allocate the required address or addresses while preparing a DRA `ResourceClaim`, before the device is configured for the Pod. The allocated addresses must be exposed through the claim's allocated-device status so that the result is inspectable and can be restored. - Make claim operations idempotent. Retrying preparation must preserve the existing allocation rather than consume another address. Cilium component restarts must not change live allocations, and a partially failed preparation must roll back any newly allocated addresses. - Release addresses when the claim is unprepared and they are no longer used. Stale capacity must be reclaimed safely when nodes or claims disappear. - Handle concurrent claims without duplicate live allocations within the same address space. Missing configuration, address-family mismatches, and exhaustion must leave the claim unprepared and surface an actionable, retryable error. - Scale across large node counts and high claim churn without allocation latency or API-server and control-plane load becoming a bottleneck. Unused capacity must be reclaimable safely. - Cover the allocation, retry, restart/restore, rollback, release, exhaustion, IPv4, IPv6, and dual-stack paths with automated tests and document the operational lifecycle. ### Scope and non-goals This issue is limited to IP address management for network devices handled by the Cilium Network Driver. It does not propose changes to device discovery, DRA scheduling, SR-IOV or other device-manager behavior, VLAN or route configuration, NRI integration, or Cilium datapath connectivity for the secondary interface. It also does not replace existing Pod IPAM modes or track static address assignment. ### Notify relevant community channels @cilium/network-driver @cilium/sig-ipam
signals.author: pippolo84

signals.title: BPF masquerade drops IPv6 Router Solicitations and Advertisements on nodes whose masquerade address is a link-local
signals.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version Observed on v1.19.4, but this is not a version-specific bug: the ICMPv6 punt list in `snat_v6_nat()` is byte-for-byte identical in v1.19.4, v1.19.6, v1.20.0 and `main`, so every supported release is affected. I picked the exact-version fields below over the dropdown for that reason rather than to skip the upgrade check. ### What happened? On a node whose only IPv6 address on the selected devices is a link-local, IPv6 Router Solicitations and Router Advertisements emitted by the node are dropped by BPF masquerade: ``` xx drop (Unsupported protocol for NAT masquerade, -1) flow 0x0 , file nodeport_egress.h:152, identity host->unknown: fe80::bae9:24ff:fe80:ebfe -> ff02::1 icmp RouterAdvertisement ``` The chain is: 1. When no selected device has a global IPv6 address, the best IPv6 fallback node address is the link-local itself. `fallbackAddresses.update()` ranks candidates by public-vs-private and scope and does not exclude link-locals, so `bpfMasqAddrs()` hands that link-local to the datapath as `nat_ipv6_masquerade`. 2. RS/RA are always sourced from a link-local, so `__snat_v6_needs_masquerade()` matches such a packet on its very first test — source equals the masquerade address — and answers `NAT_NEEDED`. 3. That leaves `snat_v6_nat()` nothing but the ICMPv6 type to go on: it only consults `snat_v6_nat_can_skip()` for TCP/UDP/SCTP. It punts echo replies, redirects and NS/NA to the stack and returns `DROP_NAT_UNSUPP_PROTO` for everything else, including RS and RA. Expected: RS/RA reach the wire untranslated. Neighbor Discovery is link-local by definition and must never be masqueraded — rewriting an RA's source would advertise the masquerade address as the router's link-local. RFC 4890 §4.4, which 5244b68c1468 ("bpf: Hande icmpv6 in host firewall") cites when it added the NS/NA punt, lists RS/RA in the same must-not-be-dropped group. I hit this doing BGP unnumbered peering, where the node emits RAs out a Cilium-managed native device and the FRR peer will not accept an unnumbered neighbor whose link-local it has not learned from those RAs — but nothing about the drop is specific to BGP; any RA sender on such a node is affected. ### How can we reproduce the issue? 1. Install Cilium with BPF masquerade and IPv6 enabled: `--set enableIPv6Masquerade=true --set bpf.masquerade=true --set ipv6.enabled=true` 2. Use a node where none of the selected devices has a global IPv6 address, only a link-local, so the chosen `nat_ipv6_masquerade` is that link-local. Confirm with `cilium-dbg statedb node-addresses` / the agent's masquerade address in `cilium-dbg status`. 3. Emit an RA out that device from the host netns (radvd, `zebra`, or a crafted packet). 4. `cilium-dbg monitor --type drop` shows the drop above. A BPF unit test reproduces it without a cluster; it ships with the fix as `bpf/tests/host_bpf_masq_linklocal.c` and sets `nat_ipv6_masquerade` to the node's link-local and sends an RA and an RS through the host egress program. ### Cilium Version ``` Client: 1.19.4 go version go1.25.10 linux/amd64 Daemon: 1.19.4 go version go1.25.10 linux/amd64 ``` This is a build off the v1.19.4 tag carrying my in-flight BGP-unnumbered patches from #47394. None of them touch the NAT code — `bpf/lib/nat.h` is stock v1.19.4 here. ### Kernel Version ``` Linux node1 6.17.9-45-g435a44e1-coreweave-amd64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Thu Apr 9 14:24:27 UTC 2026 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux ``` ### Kubernetes Version ``` Client Version: v1.36.3 Kustomize Version: v5.8.1 Server Version: v1.35.4 ``` ### Regression Not a regression — the ICMPv6 punt list in `snat_v6_nat()` has never included RS/RA. It was added for NS/NA in 5244b68c1468. ### Anything else? A fix is on the way; it is being split out of #47394 into its own PR, which I will link here.
signals.author: ecbaldwin

signals.title: Connected UDP sockets remain pinned to deleted CoreDNS backends after Pod IP changes
signals.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version Cilium 1.17.3 ### What happened? When Cilium Socket-LB is enabled, NGINX connected UDP DNS sockets may be rewritten from the Kubernetes DNS Service IP to a CoreDNS Pod IP. Initially, after CoreDNS Pods were restarted and received new IP addresses, some existing NGINX UDP sockets continued to show the old CoreDNS Pod IP. During this period, NGINX DNS resolution could fail until NGINX was reloaded. However, the issue is intermittent and is no longer reproducible after reloading NGINX. After running: ```bash nginx -s reload subsequent CoreDNS Pod IP changes are handled correctly. Cilium Socket-LB removes the old backend IP, and newly created sockets use the current CoreDNS backend. ## Observed Result Before the NGINX reload, stale backend IPs were observed intermittently. After the NGINX reload: - The issue could no longer be reproduced. - Cilium Socket-LB cleaned up the old CoreDNS backend IP. - Newly created NGINX sockets used the current CoreDNS backend. - DNS resolution continued to work after subsequent CoreDNS Pod IP changes. ## Expected Behavior Cilium should clean up or re-evaluate connected UDP sockets when a CoreDNS backend Pod is deleted, without requiring an NGINX reload. The behavior should be consistent regardless of whether NGINX has recently been reloaded. ### How can we reproduce the issue? ## Reproduction Steps 1. Run NGINX for an extended period so that connected UDP DNS sockets are created. 2. Check the sockets: ss -up The peer may show a CoreDNS Pod IP instead of the DNS Service IP: <NGINX_POD_IP>:<SOURCE_PORT> -> <OLD_COREDNS_POD_IP>:53 3. Restart the CoreDNS Deployment: kubectl -n kube-system rollout restart deployment/coredns kubectl -n kube-system rollout status deployment/coredns The actual Deployment name may be coredns or kube-dns. 4. Confirm that the CoreDNS Pod IPs have changed. 5. Check the NGINX sockets again: ss -up 6. In the initial state, some sockets continued to show the old CoreDNS Pod IP. 7. NGINX reported errors similar to: could not be resolved (5: Operation refused) 8. Reload NGINX: nginx -s reload 9. Repeat the CoreDNS restart and Pod IP change. ### Cilium Version ## Environment - Cilium: 1.17.3 - Kubernetes: managed Kubernetes cluster - KubeProxyReplacement: enabled - Socket-LB: enabled - Socket-LB coverage: Full - Load-balancing mode: SNAT - Workload: NGINX - DNS backend: CoreDNS - DNS Service: kube-dns - DNS Service ClusterIP: <KUBE_DNS_SERVICE_IP> NGINX configuration: resolver <KUBE_DNS_SERVICE_IP> valid=5s ipv6=off; ### Kernel Version ## Environment - Cilium: 1.17.3 - Kubernetes: managed Kubernetes cluster - KubeProxyReplacement: enabled - Socket-LB: enabled - Socket-LB coverage: Full - Load-balancing mode: SNAT - Workload: NGINX - DNS backend: CoreDNS - DNS Service: kube-dns - DNS Service ClusterIP: <KUBE_DNS_SERVICE_IP> NGINX configuration: resolver <KUBE_DNS_SERVICE_IP> valid=5s ipv6=off; ### Kubernetes Version ## Environment - Cilium: 1.17.3 - Kubernetes: managed Kubernetes cluster - KubeProxyReplacement: enabled - Socket-LB: enabled - Socket-LB coverage: Full - Load-balancing mode: SNAT - Workload: NGINX - DNS backend: CoreDNS - DNS Service: kube-dns - DNS Service ClusterIP: <KUBE_DNS_SERVICE_IP> NGINX configuration: resolver <KUBE_DNS_SERVICE_IP> valid=5s ipv6=off; ### Regression _No response_ ### Sysdump _No response_ ### Relevant log output ```shell ``` ### Anything else? _No response_ ### Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? Please add yourself to the [Users doc](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/USERS.md) ### Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signals.title: CFP: Gateway API TLS Options
signals.text: ### Is your proposed feature related to a problem? Currently, Cilium does not provide a way to configure TLS protocol versions or cipher suites for Gateway API listeners. The Gateway API specification already provides an extension point for implementation-specific per-listener TLS configuration through `spec.listeners[].tls.options`, but Cilium does not consume these options today. These options should apply to both `Gateway` listeners and `ListenerSet` listeners. ### Describe the feature you'd like Add support for Cilium-specific TLS listener options under `spec.listeners[].tls.options`. A minimal implementation should support TLS version controls: ```yaml cilium.io/tls-min-version: "" cilium.io/tls-max-version: "" ``` A broader implementation can also support advanced TLS controls that map to Envoy TLS Parameters: ```yaml cilium.io/tls-cipher-suites: "" cilium.io/tls-ecdh-curves: "" cilium.io/tls-signature-algorithms: "" ``` ### Notify relevant community channels @cilium/sig-servicemesh ### (Optional) Describe your proposed solution _No response_

signals.title: Helm chart support for removing port 80 in cilium-ingress
signals.text: ### Is your proposed feature related to a problem? Yes - port 80 is hardcoded ### Describe the feature you'd like The Service of the Cilium Ingress Controller, cilium-ingress hardcodes Port 80. This translates into a Port 80 listener on the AWS LoadBalancer, which violates our AWS Policy and the LoadBalancer is deleted within 2 hours. To avoid this, it would be nice if there was support in the helm chart to omit port 80 when ingress activated. In the meantime, we have resolved this with a MutatingAdmissionPolicy an a Job ### Notify relevant community channels @cilium ### (Optional) Describe your proposed solution it would be nice if there was support in the helm chart to omit port 80 when ingress activated

signals.title: NeighborDiscovery leaves stale forwardable-ip entries after node deletion
signals.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.18.12 and lower than v1.19.0 ### What happened? ## Description A node was deleted: `stage-jfpsf-wn5kt` However, the `forwardable-ip` table still contains an entry owned by the deleted node: ```text cilium shell 'db/get forwardable-ip 10.23.35.70' IP Owners 10.23.35.70 node:default/stage-jfpsf-wn5kt ``` The corresponding kernel neighbor entry also remains: ```text ip neigh | grep 10.23.35.70 10.23.35.70 dev eth0 managed extern_learn INCOMPLETE ``` After some time it may transition to `FAILED`, but it is not removed. The node itself is no longer present, but the stale `forwardable-ip` owner keeps the neighbor entry alive. ## Expected behavior When the node is deleted, NeighborDiscovery should remove the node owner from the `forwardable-ip` table. If there are no remaining owners for the IP, the corresponding desired/kernel neighbor entry should eventually be removed as well. ## Actual behavior The deleted node remains as an owner of the `forwardable-ip` entry: ```text node:default/stage-jfpsf-wn5kt ``` and the kernel neighbor remains: ```text 10.23.35.70 dev eth0 managed extern_learn INCOMPLETE ``` or later: ```text 10.23.35.70 dev eth0 managed extern_learn FAILED ``` The stale neighbor is never cleaned up. ## Impact The stale neighbor causes repeated ARP resolution attempts for an IP that belongs to a deleted node. With multiple stale entries, this generates a significant amount of unnecessary ARP traffic. In our environment, many deleted-node IPs remain in `FAILED/INCOMPLETE` state and continuously generate ARP requests, increasing broadcast packet rate on the L2 network. ### How can we reproduce the issue? config ``` data: agent-not-ready-taint-key: node.cilium.io/agent-not-ready annotate-k8s-node: "true" auto-direct-node-routes: "true" bpf-ct-global-tcp-max: "1048576" bpf-distributed-lru: "false" bpf-events-drop-enabled: "true" bpf-events-policy-verdict-enabled: "true" bpf-events-trace-enabled: "true" bpf-lb-acceleration: disabled bpf-lb-algorithm: maglev bpf-lb-algorithm-annotation: "false" bpf-lb-dsr-dispatch: opt bpf-lb-external-clusterip: "false" bpf-lb-map-max: "65536" bpf-lb-mode: dsr bpf-lb-mode-annotation: "false" bpf-lb-sock: "false" bpf-lb-source-range-all-types: "false" bpf-map-dynamic-size-ratio: "0.005" bpf-nat-global-max: "524288" bpf-policy-map-max: "65536" bpf-policy-stats-map-max: "65536" bpf-root: /sys/fs/bpf cgroup-root: /run/cilium/cgroupv2 cilium-endpoint-gc-interval: 5m0s cluster-id: "0" cluster-name: default cluster-pool-ipv4-cidr: 10.86.128.0/17 cluster-pool-ipv4-mask-size: "26" clustermesh-enable-endpoint-sync: "false" clustermesh-enable-mcs-api: "false" cni-exclusive: "true" cni-log-file: /var/run/cilium/cilium-cni.log controller-group-metrics: write-cni-file sync-host-ips sync-lb-maps-with-k8s-services custom-cni-conf: "false" datapath-mode: veth debug: "false" debug-verbose: "" default-lb-service-ipam: lbipam devices: eth+ direct-routing-device: "" direct-routing-skip-unreachable: "false" signals.title: Persistent traffic drops after 1.18.10 → 1.19.5 upgrade - warning log "Skipping named port" for all named-port ingress rules
signals.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.19.6 and lower than v1.20.0 ### What happened? During an in-place upgrade from 1.18.10 → 1.19.5, cilium pods were restarted as the Daemonset executed a `RollingUpdate`. One of the cilium-agent pods restarted with a bad state, causing all ingress traffic to be dropped for workloads on that node. The issue was only resolved after the pod was manually restarted. Upon upgrade, the problematic cilium-agent pod restarted and restored its existing endpoints (~18 endpoints total). During endpoint restore/regeneration, the agent: 1. Unpinned and recreated every per-endpoint policy map (`cilium_policy_v2_*`). I think this part is expected and benign because I see the `PolicyEntry` value struct changed between [`v1.18.10`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/v1.18.10/pkg/maps/policymap/policymap.go) and [`v1.19.5`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/v1.19.5/pkg/maps/policymap/policymap.go). 2. Emitted `Skipping named port` logs for the full set of named ports across all workload endpoints. ### Theory Regeneration logs reported success (`regenerated=18 failed=0`), but the named-port ingress allow rules were not programmed. The `Skipping named port` warnings were emitted once and regeneration was never retried, so the endpoints remained misconfigured. ### Additional context * The cluster uses a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy to implement a "default-deny" stance for all workloads in the namespace * Each workload defines its own CiliumNetworkPolicy to enable ingress and egress and those policies use L4 rules that reference named ports * [Policy enforcement](https://docs.cilium.io/en/latest/security/policy/intro/) is set to `default` mode ### How can we reproduce the issue? Unsure. It seems to be a race condition give that we saw this behavior on only 3 pods out of 1,800+ pods across various clusters. ### Cilium Version 1.19.5 ### Kernel Version 6.12.94-123.180.amzn2023.x86_64 ### Kubernetes Version 1.33 ### Regression Yes, this seems to be unique to the rule regeneration behavior for version 1.19. Our team cannot say we have definitely observed this problem during previous upgrades. ### Sysdump Not available. The affected `cilium-agent` pod was manually deleted to remediate the outage before a sysdump was captured. ### Relevant log output ```shell time=… level=info msg="Regenerating restored endpoints" module=agent.controlplane.endpoint-restore restored=18 time=… level=info msg="Unpinning map with incompatible properties" \ bpfMapPath=/sys/fs/bpf/tc/globals/cilium_policy_v2_0<ID> \ old="[type LPMTrie keySize 12 valueSize 8 maxEntries 32768 flags 1]" \ new="[type LPMTrie keySize 12 valueSize 12 maxEntries 32768 flags 129]" time=… level=warn msg="Skipping named port" \ ciliumEndpointName=<ns>/<pod> endpointID=<id> k8sPodName=<ns>/<pod> \ subsys=endpoint error="nil map" portName=broker protocol=TCP trafficDirection=ingress time=… level=info msg="Finished regenerating restored endpoints" \ module=agent.controlplane.endpoint-restore regenerated=18 failed=0 ``` ### Anything else? Here is a subset of the configuration from our Helm values file: ``` cni: chainingMode: portmap egressMasqueradeInterfaces: eth+ en+ enableIPv4Masquerade: true encryption: enabled: true nodeEncryption: false type: ipsec eni: enabled: true ipam: mode: eni routingMode: native ``` ### Cilium Users Document - [x] Are you a user of Cilium? signals.title: gateway-api: Implement FrontendTLSValidation for downstream mTLS
signals.text: ## Summary Implements GEP-91 FrontendTLSValidation support in Cilium's Gateway API to enable downstream mTLS, where the gateway validates client certificates before allowing connections. ### Key Changes - **Model Layer**: Added `FrontendTLSValidation` struct to hold mTLS configuration with `CACertRefs` and `RequireClientCertificate` fields - **Ingestion Layer**: Added `toFrontendTLSValidation()` to parse Gateway API FrontendTLSValidation from `Gateway.Spec.TLS.Frontend` - **Translation Layer**: Modified `toTransportSocket()` to configure Envoy's `DownstreamTlsContext` with `RequireClientCertificate` and `ValidationContextSdsSecretConfig` - **ConfigMap Sync**: Added functions to sync Frontend TLS CA certificate ConfigMaps to the secrets namespace - **Gateway Reconciler**: Added validation for Frontend TLS ConfigMap references (existence, `ca.crt` key, ReferenceGrant permissions) - **Gateway Watcher**: Added ConfigMap watcher to trigger reconciliation on CA certificate changes ### Target Envoy Config ```yaml transportSocket: name: envoy.transport_sockets.tls typedConfig: '@type': type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.transport_sockets.tls.v3.DownstreamTlsContext requireClientCertificate: true # Based on Mode (AllowValidOnly vs AllowInsecureFallback) commonTlsContext: tlsCertificateSdsSecretConfigs: [...] # Server certs (existing) validationContextSdsSecretConfig: # NEW: Client CA certs name: cilium-secrets/namespace-cfgmap-ca-name ``` ### Supported Configuration - `Gateway.Spec.TLS.Frontend.Default.Validation` - Default mTLS config for all HTTPS listeners - `Gateway.Spec.TLS.Frontend.PerPort[].TLS.Validation` - Per-port overrides - `AllowValidOnly` mode - Requires valid client certificate - `AllowInsecureFallback` mode - Allows connections without valid cert ## Test plan - [x] Unit tests for `toFrontendTLSValidation()` covering all validation modes - [x] All existing tests pass - [x] Manual testing with Gateway configured with mTLS - [x] Verify client with valid cert can connect - [x] Verify client without cert is rejected (AllowValidOnly) or allowed (AllowInsecureFallback) ## Related Issues Implements GEP-91 (Gateway API FrontendTLSValidation)

signals.title: daemon: fall back to API server when pod is missing from cache during restore
signals.text: During agent restarts or rolling updates, the pod informer cache can experience eventual consistency delays when pulling data from the API server's internal watch cache. This occasionally causes `getPodForEndpoint` to fail cache lookups for valid pods, skipping endpoint restoration. The orphaned endpoints are subsequently deleted by the `stale-endpoint-cleanup` routine. This commit prevents premature endpoint drops by modifying `getPodForEndpoint` to fall back to a direct Kubernetes API server query if a pod cache miss occurs. To enable testing of this workflow without spinning up a heavy daemon: - Converted `endpointRestorer.k8sWatcher` into a lightweight internal interface. - Added unit tests in `endpoint_restore_test.go` isolating the fallback logic. signals.title: bandwidth: support DSCP marking for Pod egress traffic
signals.text: This PR adds support for setting DSCP marks on Pod egress traffic through the Bandwidth Manager. Pods can configure the DSCP value with the `bandwidth.cilium.io/egress-dscp` annotation. The annotation accepts values in the `0-63` range. The BPF datapath preserves the existing ECN bits while rewriting the IPv4 TOS or IPv6 Traffic Class field. The feature is held behind `--enable-dscp-marking` / `bandwidthManager.dscp.enabled`, and requires the Bandwidth Manager to be enabled. Then annotate a Pod, e.g. for Expedited Forwarding (DSCP 46): ```yaml metadata: annotations: bandwidth.cilium.io/egress-dscp: "46" ``` Follow ups: - Tunnel outer-header DSCP marking is not included in this PR and will be covered separately. - User-facing documentation will be added in a follow-up PR. Refs: #43150 ```release-note Add support for setting DSCP marks on Pod egress traffic through the Bandwidth Manager using the `bandwidth.cilium.io/egress-dscp` annotation. ```

signals.title: datapath/l2responder: use l3 socket for v6 solicited node responder
signals.text: the l2 responder allows cilium to respond for non local ips (ex: service VIPs) by opening a l2 socket over the iface, which in turn programs the nic filtering to let ipv6 solicited node requests to be passed up the stack. this works well under the assumption that the solicited node multicasts are always flooded, but in case of an upstream switch that does MLD snooping, traffic is not flooded unless the node explicitly joins the group. this commit changes the layer2 socket approach with a l3 socket approach, so MLD joins are sent out whenever the agent needs to respond for a particular address. Fixes: #46274 ```release-note datapath/l2responder: use l3 sockets for solicited node multicast signaling ``` [AI Influence Level]: https://danielmiessler.com/blog/ai-influence-level-ail AIL 2 [Cilium AI Policy]: https://github.com/cilium/community/blob/main/AI-POLICY.md [Developer’s Certificate of Origin]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#dev-coo [Submitting a pull request]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#submitting-a-pull-request

signals.title: allow cni channing generic veth to use bandwidth QoS
signals.text: ## Problem In CNI chaining mode (generic-veth, e.g. behind Kube-OVN), pod-ingress traffic is delivered to the pod veth directly by the chained CNI and reaches `cil_to_container`. It never traverses `local_delivery()`, which is the only place the ingress token-bucket policer (`accept()`) runs today. As a result, `kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth` QoS is silently not enforced for chained pods. ## Change - Apply the ingress bandwidth policer in `cil_to_container` for the generic-veth chaining case. The new site and the existing `local_delivery()` site are made mutually exclusive (gated on the chaining mode) so a packet is metered exactly once; otherwise a packet delivered via `local_delivery()` and then egressing the lxc device would be metered twice, halving the configured ingress rate. BPF host routing delivers via `redirect_peer()` and bypasses `cil_to_container`, hence the `!ENABLE_HOST_ROUTING` guard. - Convert `ENABLE_BANDWIDTH_MANAGER` from a compile-time `#define` into a node-level runtime config `CONFIG(enable_bandwidth_manager)`, in line with the ongoing migration of datapath configuration away from `#defines`. Its value is sourced from the bandwidth manager's post-probe state (`Manager.Enabled()`), threaded through the local node configuration like `EnableWireguard`/`EnableIPSec`, so it stays false when the manager disables itself (IPsec, unreadable procfs, …). Verifier/complexity coverage is preserved by exercising the toggle as a load-time permutation in `verifier_load_test.go`. ```release-note Enforce ingress bandwidth QoS (kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth) for pods using generic-veth CNI chaining. ``` # About AIL AIL:2 — I designed the feature and the datapath change; AI assistance was used for rebasing onto latest main, merge-conflict resolution, formatting cleanup and commit hygiene. I personally reviewed every change (bpf_lxc.c gating, edt.h/token_bucket.h runtime CONFIG conversion, Makefile/complexity-tests) and verified the build, BPF verifier permutations and unit tests locally.

signals.title: gateway-api: add support for ExtensionRef using Envoy ext_proc filter
signals.text: Add support for Gateway API `ExtensionRef` filters backed by a new typed `CiliumEnvoyExtProcFilter` CRD. This lets HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute attach Envoy `ext_proc` filters without requiring users to author raw `CiliumEnvoyConfig`. This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally reviewed each line of the submission. In addition to the Cilium Makefile validations, I ran tests in a live kind cluster that can be found here: https://github.com/eufriction/k8s-cilium-gapi#test-results-by-version. The implementation currently includes: - a namespaced `CiliumEnvoyExtProcFilter` - Gateway API ingestion and translation support for HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute `ExtensionRef` filters - feature-falgs for Helm and operator - ReferenceGrant enforcement and route status reporting for cross-namespace ext_proc backends - Envoy ext_proc metrics - unit/golden-file coverage plus user-facing documentation and examples. Design notes: - Envoy `ext_proc` filters are inserted before `ext_autz`. - I think the best long-term solution is to have a placement strategy with support for First, BeforeAuth, AfterAuth, and Last. This will not be included in this PR until more feedback from the community arrives as @youngnick suggest. - For this PR, Cilium resolves the order using Gateway API precedence: oldest route creation timestamp wins, followed by namespace/name and filter index. - Surfacing conflicts through a Gateway API status condition is not done yet. Could maybe wait for #46681? - Unresolved or invalid ext_proc BackendRefs fail closed. The affected route receives a configuration error and a 500 DirectResponse Fixes: #45951 ```release-note Gateway API HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute filters can reference CiliumEnvoyExtProcFilter resources via ExtensionRef to configure Envoy ext_proc filters. ```

signals.title: bgp: gate BGP announcements on host datapath init
signals.text: ## Description The BGP Control Plane controller starts reconciling as soon as the CiliumNode resource becomes available, which happens before `bpf_host.c` has been attached to native devices. On node reboot, this caused a "No route to host" window: the upstream router added the node back to its ECMP group, but incoming LB traffic arrived on native devices with no BPF program to DNAT it. Fix by blocking `Run()` on `Loader.HostDatapathInitialized()` before entering the event loop. The channel is closed by `ReloadDatapath()` once the host endpoint BPF programs have been attached. `Loader` is already available in the Hive dependency graph and is injected via `ControllerParams`. ## Reproduction **Setup** - Two nodes acting as BGP ECMP peers for a LoadBalancer service (`externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster`) - Upstream router distributes traffic across both nodes via ECMP - Build Cilium with a `time.Sleep(30 * time.Second)` added at the top of `ReloadDatapath()` in `pkg/datapath/loader/endpoint.go`, and deploy the modified image as the cilium-agent on both nodes **Steps to reproduce** 1. Reboot one of the two nodes 2. Send requests to the LoadBalancer VIP from an external client during the 30-second window after the rebooted node's BGP session re-establishes **Observed behavior** "No route to host" errors occur during the window. Depending on which ECMP bucket the client's 5-tuple hashes to, the failure rate should be either 100% or 0% per flow. **Expected behavior** No errors: BGP should not advertise routes until BPF programs are attached to native devices. ```release-note Fix a "No route to host" window on node reboot where BGP advertised routes before BPF programs were attached to native devices. ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked the datapath attachment sequence and the HostDatapathInitialized channel lifecycle.

Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! Fixes: trafficDistribution hints on non-active backends ## Summary - This PR was prepared with AIL:2. I personally implemented fix in code, used AI for tests and better descriptions. - With `trafficDistribution: PreferSameNode` and a single node-local backend (e.g. a DaemonSet), restarting that local backend causes a multi-second window where an in-cluster client on the same node gets `connection refused` instead of falling back to a ready remote backend. - The drain side works correctly: while the old local Pod is `Terminating`, traffic falls back to remote backends. The drop happens only on the **return** side — while the replacement Pod is starting. During startup the replacement backend is programmed in `BackendStateMaintenance`, and `topologyPreferenceCandidate` does not exclude that state, so `PreferSameNode` treats it as a valid same-node candidate, commits to "same-node only", and pins traffic to a backend that cannot yet serve. - This is the startup-side analogue of the draining-side bug fixed for `Terminating` backends in #46339. That fix excluded `Terminating`/`TerminatingNotServing` (states 1/2); the candidate check still accepts `Quarantined` (3) and `Maintenance` (4), and a starting backend lands in `Maintenance` (4). ### Current behaviour - During drain of the old local Pod: requests fall back to a remote backend (correct, no drop). - While the replacement Pod is starting: `connection refused` for the whole starting window, instead of continued fallback to a remote backend. Recovery coincides with the new Pod becoming Ready. ### Expected - While the returning same-node backend is not yet serving, `PreferSameNode` should keep falling back to ready remote backends (as it already does during drain), then snap back to the local backend once it is serving. No connection-refused window. ## PR-implemented fix - Require `Active` state for topology-preference candidacy even for non-health-checked services. - This subsumes the existing terminating checks and also excludes `Maintenance`/`Quarantined`. signals.title: lbmap: display proxy port for L7 services
signals.text: ## lbmap: display proxy port for L7 services When dumping entries from `cilium_lb4_services_v2`, L7 service entries are currently displayed using the `BackendID` field. For L7 services, however, this field does not represent a backend ID. It stores the Envoy proxy port in network byte order. Since `Service4Value.String()` prints the raw field directly, the displayed value is byte-swapped on little-endian systems, making the output misleading. This PR detects L7 service entries via the `L7LB` service flag and displays the decoded proxy port instead, so that the output reflects the actual forwarding destination. ## Reproducer Create a Gateway API service backed by the Cilium L7 proxy. ```console $ kubectl get svc -n horizon-system cilium-gateway-horizon-gateway NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) cilium-gateway-horizon-gateway LoadBalancer 10.43.2.169 10.251.8.82 80:32201/TCP ``` The Envoy proxy allocated for this Gateway is listening on port `18036`: ```console $ netstat -anp | grep cilium-envoy | grep LISTEN tcp 0 0 127.0.0.1:18036 0.0.0.0:* LISTEN 2472775/cilium-envoy ``` The allocated proxy port is also recorded in Cilium's proxy state: ```console $ cat /var/run/cilium/state/proxy_ports_state.json { "horizon-system/cilium-gateway-horizon-gateway/listener": { "type": "crd", "ingress": false, "port": 18036 } } ``` However, dumping the service map shows: ```console $ cilium map get cilium_lb4_services_v2 | grep 10.251.8.82 10.251.8.82:80/TCP (0) 29766 0[0] (204) [0x60 0x4] ``` The value `29766` is not the actual proxy port. It is the raw network-byte-order representation of `18036` interpreted as a host-order integer. As a result, the output can be confusing when troubleshooting L7 load balancer entries. ## Root Cause For L7 service entries, the value stored in `BackendID` is actually the Envoy proxy port encoded in network byte order. `Service4Value.String()` always prints the raw `BackendID` field, so the proxy port is displayed incorrectly on little-endian architectures. ## Fix This PR updates `Service4Value.String()` to detect L7 service entries using the `L7LB` service flag. Instead of printing the raw `BackendID` field, it uses `GetL7LBProxyPort()` to decode the stored value into host byte order before formatting the output. ### Before ```console 10.251.8.82:80/TCP (0) 29766 0[0] (204) [0x60 0x4] ``` ### After ```console 10.251.8.82:80/TCP (0) 18036 0[0] (204) [0x60 0x4] ``` This change only affects the string representation used when dumping service map entries. It does not modify datapath behavior or the contents of the BPF maps.

signals.title: bpf: Enable extended masquerade port range for BPF masquerade
signals.text: Under heavy outbound egress traffic, pods undergoing BPF masquerading can experience SNAT port exhaustion when restricted to the standard port range (`32768-65535`). This is a particular concern for users migrating from Kubernetes ip-masq-agent to Cilium eBPF masquerade, because the two have different default source port ranges: - Cilium eBPF masquerade selects any port in `32768-65535` by default. - Kubernetes ip-masq-agent selects any port in `1024-65535` by default. This change introduces support for configuring an extended masquerade port range (`--node-port-nat-range-ext`, e.g. `1024,29999`) across IPv4 and IPv6 to achieve source port range parity: 1. Refactor NAT Port Ranges into Runtime Config: - Replaced compile-time `#define NODEPORT_PORT_MIN/MAX_NAT` with dynamic BPF runtime config variables (`nodeport_port_min_nat` and `nodeport_port_max_nat`). 2. Extended Masquerade Port Range Support: - Added `--node-port-nat-range-ext` CLI flag in Hive loadbalancer configuration and mapped it to Helm. - Enforced validation rules (range bounds checking, ensuring non-overlap with NodePort range and privileged ports). - Implemented random port range selection in BPF for outgoing SNAT flows. - Added automatic fallback to the alternative range if the selected port range encounters allocation exhaustion. Fixes: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/23604 ```release-note bpf: Support configuring an extended masquerade port range (`--node-port-nat-range-ext`) for BPF SNAT masquerading. ``` [AI Influence Level]: https://danielmiessler.com/blog/ai-influence-level-ail [Cilium AI Policy]: https://github.com/cilium/community/blob/main/AI-POLICY.md [Developer’s Certificate of Origin]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#dev-coo [Submitting a pull request]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#submitting-a-pull-request

See the section [Developer’s Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Thanks for contributing! <!-- Description of change --> When Cilium is restarted with `enable-ztunnel=false`, in-pod iptables redirect rules left in previously enrolled pods cause traffic blackholing. To resolve this without mutating per-endpoint state serialization, this change introduces node-level state tracking via a `ztunnel_enabled` marker file persisted in `option.Config.StateDir`. When `enable-ztunnel=true`, a Hive `OnStart` lifecycle hook creates the marker file. When the agent starts with `enable-ztunnel=false`, `registerCleanup` checks for the marker: if absent, execution returns immediately as a zero-cost O(1) no-op; if present, it schedules a restore-gated one-shot job (`ztunnel-inpod-cleanup`) that awaits endpoint restoration (`WaitForEndpointRestore`), iterates restored endpoints to execute `iptables.DeleteInPodRules()` inside each pod's network namespace (gracefully skipping terminated pods via `os.ErrNotExist`), and unlinks the marker file upon full completion to guarantee retry idempotency across restarts. Fixes: #46333 ```release-note Fix traffic blackholing when disabling ztunnel by introducing node-level state tracking to automatically strip in-pod redirect rules from restored endpoints. ``` [Developer’s Certificate of Origin]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#dev-coo [Submitting a pull request]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#submitting-a-pull-request

signals.text: This PR contains some enhancements to the eBPF execution step to help improve the eBPF test suite speed discussed in #45133. During node deletion, `deallocateIDForNode` selected one matching ID and deallocated only that ID. Secondary forward/reverse mappings, BPF node-map entries, and the corresponding IDs could remain. The deletion path now collects every distinct nonzero ID from deleted-node IPs that have not been reused by another live node, then deallocates each ID exactly once. An ID returns to the pool only after its reverse set is empty, so it remains allocated if a live mapping or a BPF deletion failure remains. A multi-ID mismatch stays diagnostic-only when repair succeeds; actual cleanup failures are still returned. The related allocation/update conflict path can independently leave old IDs unreclaimed. That behavior is known and intentionally out of scope for a focused follow-up. ## Testing ```text go test ./pkg/datapath/linux -run '^TestDeallocateIDsForNode$' -count=1 go test ./pkg/datapath/linux -run '^TestDeallocateIDsForNode$' -count=100 go test ./pkg/datapath/linux -count=1 ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:3. GitHub Copilot assisted with source analysis, implementation, and test drafting. The final patch was independently reviewed, and all listed checks were run against the exact commit. Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! I've been reviewing some cases where the cilium-agent is failing to startup happliy and goes into CLB for a while on new nodes in AWS. It appears that there can be some significant latency from when the `cilium-operator` calls `AtachNetworkInterface` to when that ENI actually shows up on the node from it's kernel logs. The worst case I've found over the last 2 weeks was 149 seconds. The compounding issue is that with the current max of 3.75s + kubelet's exponetial backoff restarting the agent, where in one case the NIC was there within 129-ish seconds but, the agent wasn't able to get through this until 212-ish seconds. Okay so, with the pre-ample out of the way, this PR drops the exponential backoff and switches to using PollUntilContextTimeout instead. immediate is passed as `true` so it checks right away, so any case where the NIC is there shouldn't see any backoff. Then it'll check every second up to 150 seconds. This changes the current checking behavior from something like `0.000 0.285 0.840 1.865 3.904` (with jitter, then gives up) to `0 1 2 3 4 5 ... 150` (fixed 1s, then gives up). No chart change is required. 150s fits inside both remaining ceilings: - cilium-agent `startupProbe: failureThreshold: 300` x `periodSeconds: 2` with `initialDelaySeconds: 5` == ~600s - https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/2efb257c8533af4a446af77813d9aaa9d8b127fc/install/kubernetes/cilium/values.yaml#L2428-L2433 - `defaults.HiveStartTimeout` = 300s - https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/pkg/defaults/defaults.go#L12-L13 ```release-note ipam: Wait up to 150s for attached ENI's to show up ``` Noting too that this is related to https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/47295 and the original PR https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/41954. I had happened to be looking at this error at the same time but in prod versus CI. This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I've personally confirmed the change and backing data is all accurate by hand.

See the section [Developer's Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. **AI Disclosure (AIL:3):** I identified the need for this mode, designed the flag and Helm integration, tested both modes on a live cluster, and validated the metric, RBAC, and log behaviour. An LLM (Claude) assisted with code authoring and test writing under my full review. ## Problem The `restart-unmanaged-pods` controller is all-or-nothing: it either detects and deletes unmanaged pods (active) or is fully disabled via `--unmanaged-pod-watcher-interval=0` (no detection, no metric, no deletions). There is no intermediate state where the controller runs purely for observability — counting unmanaged pods and emitting `cilium_operator_unmanaged_pods` — without issuing pod deletions. This becomes a problem when broadening `--pod-restart-selector` beyond the default `k8s-app=kube-dns` to cover more workloads: the moment the wider selector is deployed, the controller begins deleting matching pods with no observation window. Using `--unmanaged-pod-watcher-interval=0` as a workaround disables the entire controller, so the metric is never updated and the operator emits no signal at all. ## Fix Split into two commits: **Commit 1 — Go implementation:** Add `--enable-unmanaged-pod-observe-only` (default: `false`) to `cell.go`. Wire an `observeOnly` field through `unmanagedPodsController`. In `reconcile()`, add an observe-only branch that publishes `cilium_operator_unmanaged_pods` on every cycle but skips all `Pods().Delete()` calls. The branch still evaluates restart candidates (age + per-pod cooldown) to report how many pods *would* be restarted in the log, without acting. Setting `observeOnly=true` activates the controller even when `restart=false`. The flag uses `--enable-unmanaged-pod-observe-only` rather than the issue's proposed `--unmanaged-pod-restart-enabled` to follow Cilium's `--enable-X` convention and keep it additive by default. **Commit 2 — Helm and docs:** Add `operator.unmanagedPodWatcher.observeOnly: false` to the chart. The configmap template activates the watcher when `restart OR observeOnly` is true. The `pod/delete` ClusterRole permission is omitted when `observeOnly=true` since the controller never issues deletions in that mode. Update `helm-values.rst`, `k8s-install-migration.rst`, and regenerate all `Documentation/cmdref/` files. ## Testing **Unit tests** (`operator/unmanagedpods/controller_test.go`): - `TestReconcileObserveOnly` (table-driven) — gauge accuracy across varied pod populations; zero deletions in observe-only mode - `TestReconcileObserveOnlyRepeatable` — gauge stays accurate across repeated cycles, no restart cooldown recorded - `TestReconcileObserveOnlyLogsOnlyOnCountChange` — Info log fires on eligible-count change only, suppressed on steady-state cycles **Live cluster verification:** - `observeOnly=true`: metric increments on unmanaged pod detection, zero pod deletions confirmed, `pod/delete` permission absent from operator ClusterRole - `observeOnly=false` (default): pod deleted and metric drops to 0 as expected Fixes: #46198 ```release-note Add --enable-unmanaged-pod-observe-only flag to the Cilium operator. When enabled, the unmanaged pod watcher counts and reports unmanaged pods via the cilium_operator_unmanaged_pods metric without restarting (deleting) them, enabling safe phased rollouts when broadening --pod-restart-selector.

signals.title: docs: note on eBPF ClusterIP translation vs Docker raw-table protection
signals.text: Document an interaction between Cilium's eBPF ClusterIP translation and Docker's raw-table protection that can affect hybrid Docker/Kubernetes hosts using unpublished Docker container backends. On such hosts, a `Service` backed by an unpublished Docker container can become unreachable from pods: Cilium translates the ClusterIP in the eBPF datapath, so the packet reaches Docker's `raw/PREROUTING` protection already addressed to the backend and is dropped before `DOCKER-USER`. This adds a short note to the kube-proxy-free documentation, next to the paragraph on per-packet ClusterIP load-balancing, together with a counter-based way to confirm the behaviour. Discussed and requested by a maintainer in #47601. Fixes: #47601 AI disclosure: AIL:2. Generative AI tools were used for research and technical analysis, and provided an initial draft which the author rewrote in their own words. The author independently reproduced and verified the described behaviour and takes full responsibility for the final content. ```release-note NONE ```

signals.title: helm: allow attachMetadata on the ServiceMonitors of host-network components
signals.text: ## Problem `cilium-agent`, `cilium-envoy`, `cilium-operator` and the Hubble metrics endpoint all run on the host network, so their scrape targets are node addresses. On a cluster where those node ports are not reachable from Prometheus — a closed node firewall, or nodes that are not mutually routable on the address kubelet reports — the only way to reach them is to rewrite `__address__` to an address Cilium itself publishes, such as the node's `cilium_host` address in `network.cilium.io/ipv{4,6}-cilium-host`. The chart already exposes `relabelings` for that. But a relabeling can only read labels service discovery produced, and node annotations are attached only when the ServiceMonitor sets `attachMetadata: {node: true}`. That field has no value in the chart, so the monitors cannot express it — which forces users to disable the chart's monitors entirely and hand-write equivalents outside it just to add one field. Concretely, this is what it takes today to scrape the agent on a cluster whose node ports are closed: ```yaml spec: attachMetadata: {node: true} # <- not expressible in the chart endpoints: - port: metrics relabelings: - action: replace sourceLabels: [__meta_kubernetes_node_annotation_network_cilium_io_ipv6_cilium_host] regex: (.+) replacement: "[$1]:9962" targetLabel: __address__ ``` ## Change Adds `attachMetadata` to the four `serviceMonitor` blocks whose targets are host-network, and renders it when set: - `prometheus.serviceMonitor.attachMetadata` - `operator.prometheus.serviceMonitor.attachMetadata` - `hubble.metrics.serviceMonitor.attachMetadata` - `envoy.prometheus.serviceMonitor.attachMetadata` `hubble-relay` and `clustermesh-apiserver` are deliberately not included — they are ordinary Deployments where node metadata has no use. Happy to extend for uniformity if reviewers prefer that. ## Verification - With the value set, all four ServiceMonitors render `spec.attachMetadata.node: true`. - With it unset (the default `{}`), the rendered chart is **byte-identical** to before the change. - README values table updated to match. ```release-note Added `attachMetadata` to the Helm ServiceMonitor values for cilium-agent, cilium-envoy, cilium-operator and Hubble metrics, so node labels and annotations can be used as relabeling sources when scraping these host-network components. ```
signals.author: mateo-moon

Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! <!-- Description of change --> `peerConfig` in the WireGuard agent was keeping each allowed IP in two places at once: ```go allowedIPs map[netip.Prefix]net.IPNet needsInsert map[netip.Prefix]net.IPNet needsRemove map[netip.Prefix]net.IPNet ``` The key and the value are the same prefix, just encoded differently. The `net.IPNet` half is there because `wgtypes.PeerConfig.AllowedIPs` is a `[]net.IPNet`, so the package was carrying the wgctrl representation through its own state rather than converting at the edge. This turns the three maps into sets keyed by `netip.Prefix` and moves the `net.IPNet` conversion out to the two spots that talk to wgctrl. A few other things follow from that: - `ipnetToPrefix()` called `netipx.MustFromStdIP()`, which panics if the IP is not 4 or 16 bytes. The replacement uses `netipx.FromStdIP()` and callers skip the prefix if the conversion fails. - Four blocks were building a `/32` or `/128` by hand with `net.CIDRMask()` plus an IPv4/IPv6 branch. `netip.Addr.BitLen()` already gives the right width, so those become one helper call each. Left alone on purpose: `peerConfig.nodeIPv4`/`nodeIPv6` are still `net.IP`. Converting them touches ~100 more sites in the tests and would bury this change. The `fakeWgClient` helpers and the `wgtypes.PeerConfig` literals in `cell_test.go` also stay on `net.IPNet`, since that is the API they are standing in for. Related: #24246 ## Testing `pkg/wireguard/agent` has no privileged tests, so the existing suite covers this locally end to end: ``` $ go build ./... $ go vet ./pkg/wireguard/... $ go test ./pkg/wireguard/... ok github.com/cilium/cilium/pkg/wireguard/agent 0.025s $ golangci-lint run pkg/wireguard/... 0 issues. $ gofmt -s -l pkg/wireguard/agent/ ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:1. signals.title: hubble: Add Kubernetes Pod UID to flow endpoints
signals.text: Hubble currently identifies a Pod mainly by cluster, namespace, and name. Kubernetes permits a deleted object's name to be reused, while its UID identifies that specific object lifetime. This matters especially for StatefulSet Pods, but applies to any recreated Pod. Adding the UID improves flow attribution. Consumers can distinguish Pod instances and correlate flows with Kubernetes records keyed by UID. The UID is carried through IPCache and ClusterMesh metadata, so Hubble can expose it for remote endpoints when that metadata is available. Cilium also uses the UID internally: - IPCache deletion checks UID, preventing a delayed Pod, CEP, or CES deletion from removing metadata belonging to a replacement Pod. - Same-name Pod replacements update IPCache, cgroup, endpoint, and host-network state. IPCache and NOTRACK changes install new state before removing old state, allowing a short overlap instead of a gap. - Kubernetes drop events use the UID captured in the flow instead of resolving whichever Pod currently owns that namespace/name. The UID remains optional when metadata is unavailable or components are running mixed versions. This PR was prepared with AIL:4. Codex drafted the implementation and tests. I reviewed the code and changed the replacement handling. ```release-note Hubble flow endpoints now include the Kubernetes Pod UID. ```
signals.author: devodev

signals.title: cilium-cli/connectivity: detect Cilium version in connectivity perf setup
signals.text: `cilium connectivity perf` always reports "Cilium version: 0.0.0" in its info banner, regardless of the actual Cilium version running in the cluster. `setupAndValidatePerf()`, the setup path used by the `perf` subcommand, never calls `initCiliumPods()`/`detectCiliumVersion()`, unlike `setupAndValidate()` (used by `connectivity test`). `CiliumVersion` is therefore left at its Go zero value, which prints as `0.0.0`. This calls the same two steps `setupAndValidate()` already uses, in the same order, so `CiliumVersion` is populated before it's printed in `connectivity.Run()`. Tested manually against an RKE2 cluster (Cilium v1.19.4): - before the fix, `cilium connectivity perf` reported "Cilium version: 0.0.0" - after the fix, it correctly reports "Cilium version: 1.19.4" ```release-note Fixed `cilium connectivity perf` always reporting `Cilium version: 0.0.0` instead of the actual detected Cilium version.

signals.title: install: detect GKE from kubelet path
signals.text: GKE `1.36.2-gke.2064000` no longer exposes the container runtime endpoint through the `--container-runtime-endpoint` flag in `/etc/default/kubelet`. This causes the existing node-init GKE detection to miss the GKE-specific path and fall through to generic kubelet handling. Instead of detecting individual GKE node layouts through container runtime configuration, this change uses the presence of `/home/kubernetes/bin/kubelet`, which is shared by both the legacy and current GKE layouts. The same detection is used by startup and prestop, so the kubelet wrapper installed during startup can also be detected and reverted correctly. Testing performed: * `helm lint` * Helm template rendering with GKE/node-init values * `bash -n` on rendered startup and prestop scripts * sandboxed scenarios covering legacy GKE, the GKE 1.36.2 layout, generic non-GKE nodes, and an already-installed kubelet wrapper * live GKE `1.36.2-gke.2064000` COS/containerd node verification: * `/home/kubernetes/bin/kubelet` exists as a regular executable file * `/home/kubernetes/kubelet-config.yaml` contains `containerRuntimeEndpoint: unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock` * `/etc/default/kubelet` does not contain `--container-runtime-endpoint` * `git diff --check` Claude was used to suggest the implementation. I manually reviewed the changes and validated the resulting behavior with the tests above. AIL:4 Fixes: #47884 ```release-note Fix node-init startup on GKE 1.36.2-gke.2064000 nodes by detecting GKE from the kubelet path instead of container runtime configuration. ```

signals.title: fix(bgp): only auto-discover the default gateway from the main table
signals.text: - [x] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [x] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [x] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a Fixes: #XXX line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [x] If your commit description contains a Fixes: <commit-id> tag, then please add the commit author[s] as reviewer[s] to this issue. - [x] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer’s Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! BGP peer auto-discovery in defaultGateway mode walks the whole StateDB route table and picks the default route with the lowest metric. The route table is populated from a RT_TABLE_UNSPEC netlink dump, so it holds default routes from every table, not just main — and a default route outside main is not the way off the node. This matters in practice because Cilium installs one itself. With native routing plus any of EnableEnvoyConfig, IPsec, or WireGuard, installFromProxyRoutes* adds default via <cilium_host address> dev cilium_host to table 2005 (RouteTableFromProxy) with no metric, i.e. priority 0. That outranks a real uplink default route, which typically carries a non-zero metric, so auto-discovery hands BGP the cilium_host address as the peer address and the session never comes up. Table 2004 (RouteTableToProxy) similarly holds a local default dev lo; it has no nexthop so it was already skipped, but nothing made that intentional. Restrict selection to unicast routes in the main table, which is where the node's default gateway lives. Non-unicast types (local, blackhole, unreachable, prohibit) do not forward anything either. Test changes: - A new unit case models a node with a metric-1024 main-table default route alongside a metric-0 local default dev lo in table 2004 and a metric-0 default via 10.0.5.160 in table 2005, and asserts the main-table gateway still wins. Existing default routes are built through a small defaultRouteEntry helper so every fixture carries a realistic table and type. - peering-default-gateway.txtar now sets table: 254 / type: 1 on its routes. The fixture previously left both at zero (RT_TABLE_UNSPEC / RTN_UNSPEC), which the kernel never reports for an installed route. release-note Fix BGP `defaultGateway` peer auto-discovery selecting a default route from a non-main routing table, such as the `default via cilium_host` route Cilium installs in the from-proxy table, instead of the node's real default gateway. This PR was prepared with AIL:2. I personally wrote or checked all code and validated the behavior end-to-end against a live cluster and DPU as peer (on the v1.19.x backport).

signals.title: Gateway-api: add support for session persistence
signals.text: Add cookie-based Gateway API session persistence for HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute rules as described in [CFP-47089](https://github.com/cilium/design-cfps/pull/102). Supported session persistence options are validated, with unsupported values being rejected. Accepted routes are ingested into the internal model and translated into CiliumEnvoyConfig. If a Gateway has any attached route rule containing a session persistence config, the Envoy stateful session filter is applied, alongside per-route cookie settings. Any routes attached to the Gateway without session persistence will explicitly disable the stateful session filter. The following HTTPRoute enables persistence for `/persistent`, while `/not-persistent` continues to use normal load balancing: ```yaml apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: HTTPRoute metadata: name: example-route spec: parentRefs: - name: example-gateway rules: - matches: - path: type: PathPrefix value: /persistent backendRefs: - name: example-service port: 8080 sessionPersistence: type: Cookie sessionName: app-session cookieConfig: lifetimeType: Session - matches: - path: type: PathPrefix value: /not-persistent backendRefs: - name: example-service port: 8080 ``` ```release-note Add support for Gateway API session persistence ``` AIL 2: Used to assist in planning, review, and generating some test cases.

signals.title: policy: fix wildcard CIDR selector to match host/remote-node under policyCIDRMatchMode=nodes
signals.text: ## Problem \`matchesCIDRWildcard()\` in \`pkg/policy/types/selector.go\` only checked \`option.Config.PolicyCIDRMatchesPods()\` when deciding whether a wildcard CIDR requirement (e.g. one produced from a \`0.0.0.0/0\` \`CIDRRule\`) matches a target's labels. It never checked \`PolicyCIDRMatchesNodes()\`. As a result, when \`policyCIDRMatchMode\` is set to \`nodes\` (or \`nodes,pods\`) instead of the default \`pods\`, a \`0.0.0.0/0\` egress/ingress CIDR selector would **never** match \`host\`/\`remote-node\` identities, even though \`resolveLabels()\` (in \`pkg/ipcache/metadata.go\`) does attach a CIDR label to those identities under that same configuration. The selector's wildcard-matching short-circuit and the label-attachment logic had fallen out of sync. ### Impact This breaks connectivity to any host-networked destination (kube-apiserver, apiserver-proxy, etc.) reachable only via a wildcard CIDR egress rule, whenever an operator enables \`policyCIDRMatchMode=nodes\`. We observed this concretely on OpenShift 4.22 (HyperShift-hosted clusters), where CoreDNS's egress traffic to the API server was dropped with \`Policy denied\` (`bpf_lxc.c`, drop reason \`Policy denied\`), so DNS never stabilized despite CoreDNS actually being healthy — see #48034 for the full write-up including live \`cilium-dbg monitor --type drop\` captures showing this exact failure signature. ## Fix Extend \`matchesCIDRWildcard()\` to also permit a match when the target carries the \`host\` or \`remote-node\` reserved label **and** \`PolicyCIDRMatchesNodes()\` is enabled — mirroring exactly the condition used in \`resolveLabels()\` to decide whether to attach a CIDR label to that target in the first place. ## Testing - Added two new table-driven cases to \`TestCIDRRuleToCIDRSelectors\` in \`pkg/policy/types/selector_test.go\` covering: a wildcard CIDR rule matching \`host\`/\`remote-node\` when \`policyCIDRMatchesNodes\` is enabled, and *not* matching them when disabled (existing \`pods\`-only behavior is unchanged). - Live-validated end-to-end against a real OCP 4.22 HyperShift cluster (ARO-HCP) with custom-built agent+operator images including this fix: Cilium came up healthy, all default cluster operators (network, dns, ingress, etc.) reported Available, and no \`Policy denied\` drops were observed on CoreDNS→apiserver traffic — confirming the root cause and the fix. Fixes #48034
signals.author: miquelsi

signals.title: gha/kubespray: don't wait for CoreDNS before Cilium is installed
signals.text: We run kubespray with kube_network_plugin=cni, so kubespray writes no CNI configuration and there is no pod network until Cilium is installed, yet bring-up waited for every kube-system pod to be Ready. That only worked by accident, because the old image installed podman from the Ubuntu archive and cri-dockerd picked up its /etc/cni/net.d/87-podman-bridge.conflist. The new image ships a static podman that uses netavark, leaving /etc/cni/net.d empty, so the wait can never be satisfied. Wait for the host-network control plane instead, and assert kube-system readiness after Cilium is up, where CoreDNS not converging is a real failure. Also dump cluster state on bring-up failure, since the sysdump step is skipped when Cilium was never installed. This PR was prepared with AIL:3.

signals.title: bpf: dsr: fix outer SrcIP in ICMP error msg
signals.text: By the time that we check whether a DSR request exceeds the MTU (and respond with an ICMP error msg), the request has already been DNATed to the backend IP/port (when using "opt" or "geneve" dispatch). We are currently RevNATing only the inner headers (the original request) - but the outer IP header still uses the backend's IP as sourceIP. Instead of fixing this up manually, split the code into two stages 1. RevNAT of the rejected DSR request, and then 2. use generate_icmp*_reply() to produce the ICMP msg, replacing all the custom rewrite logic. Note that for IPIP the request is in its original form at this point, and doesn't require any RevNAT processing. ```release-note When using DSR with --bpf-lb-dsr-dispatch set to "opt" or "geneve" in combination with --enable-pmtu-discovery, fix the outer source IP of the ICMP error message which is generated when a forwarded DSR request exceeds the network interface's MTU. ```

signals.title: envoy: Clarify legacy UpdateEnvoyResources
signals.text: Legacy UpdateEnvoyResources leaves the passed in `waitGroup` intentionally unused, as we need to revert changes on listener update failures also when the caller is not interested in waiting. Wait for new listeners is unconditional and satisfies the only caller's need to wait to observe listener port bind failures. Combine the wait for new Listener's dependencies (old listener removals if port number changes, new clusters) into a single WaitGroup, thus removing the reuse of the same `wg` variable for multiple waits. signals.title: gha: bound the LLVM prereq apt step with a 5m timeout
signals.text: In run 32225900868 the "Install LLVM and Clang prerequisites" step of build-commits-test hung inside apt-get for 2h51m and only stopped because the run was cancelled by hand. The step has no bound of its own, so the only thing that would have ended it is the job's timeout-minutes: 180, which burns nearly three hours of an extra-power runner before the PR reports anything. Across the last successful Build Commits runs the step completes in 6 to 18 seconds, so 5 minutes leaves plenty of headroom for a slow mirror while still failing fast when apt wedges. A hung apt is not something a retry inside the step can recover from, so failing the job and letting it be re-run is the right outcome. This PR was prepared with AIL:3.

signals.title: mac: Make `mac.MAC` a `[6]byte`
signals.text: This PR migrates `pkg/mac.MAC` from being a [`net.HardwareAddr`](https://pkg.go.dev/net#HardwareAddr) (which is a `[]byte`) to being a `[6]byte`. Why we can do this: `net.HardwareAddr` has to be a slice because it has to support MAC address representations under different formats/size, such as the 20-octet IP over InfiniBand link-layer one. Cilium has always been stricter in the MAC addresses it accepts and already enforced the IEEE 802 MAC-48 format (see `mac.MAC`'s existing docstring: "MAC address is an net.HardwareAddr encapsulation to force cilium to only use MAC-48.") What we gain from doing this: We already wanted MAC-48-only format before, now this is guaranteed and enforced by the type itself, meaning we don't need to validate the value in as many places because once we have a valid `mac.MAC`, we know it's a 48 MAC. Switching from a slice to an array also means `MAC` becomes comparable (`m1 == m2`) and can be used as map keys (`map[mac.MAC]string` for example). From a memory point of view, an array is also better than a slice, but at this scale, the gain is probably not measurable. Overall, `[6]byte` is to `net.HardwareAddr` what `netip.Addr`/`netip.Prefix` are to `net.IP`/`net.IPNet`.

signals.title: fix(bpf): don't drop IPv6 RS/RAs when masquerading
signals.text: Please ensure your pull request adheres to the following guidelines: - [x] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [x] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [x] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a `Fixes: #XXX` line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [ ] If your commit description contains a `Fixes: <commit-id>` tag, then please add the commit author[s] as reviewer[s] to this issue. - [x] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer’s Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! `snat_v6_nat()` punts ICMPv6 echo replies, redirects and NS/NA to the stack but returns `DROP_NAT_UNSUPP_PROTO` for every other type, so Router Solicitations and Advertisements do not survive the egress masquerade path: ``` xx drop (Unsupported protocol for NAT masquerade, -1) flow 0x0 , file nodeport_egress.h:152, identity host->unknown: fe80::bae9:24ff:fe80:ebfe -> ff02::1 icmp RouterAdvertisement ``` This hits a node whose only IPv6 address is a link-local. RS/RA are always sourced from a link-local, and when no selected device has a global IPv6 address the best IPv6 fallback node address is the link-local itself — `fallbackAddresses.update()` ranks candidates by public-vs-private and scope, and does not exclude link-locals — so `bpfMasqAddrs()` hands that address to the datapath as `nat_ipv6_masquerade`. `__snat_v6_needs_masquerade()` then matches such a packet on its very first test, source equals the masquerade address, and answers `NAT_NEEDED`. That leaves `snat_v6_nat()` nothing but the ICMPv6 type to go on: it only consults `snat_v6_nat_can_skip()` for TCP/UDP/SCTP. Neighbor Discovery is link-local by definition and must never be masqueraded — rewriting an RA's source would advertise the masquerade address as the router's link-local. RFC 4890 section 4.4, which 5244b68c1468 ("bpf: Hande icmpv6 in host firewall") cites when it added the NS/NA punt, lists RS/RA in the same must-not-be-dropped group. Punt them to the stack alongside NS/NA, and cover both types with a BPF masquerade test for a node whose masquerade address is a link-local. Split out of #47394 so it can be reviewed and merged on its own; it is a standalone datapath fix that does not depend on the rest of that series. Fixes: #48093 ```release-note Fix IPv6 Router Solicitations and Router Advertisements being dropped with "Unsupported protocol for NAT masquerade" on nodes whose BPF masquerade address is a link-local address. ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:2. I personally wrote or checked all code and validated the behavior end-to-end against a live cluster and DPU (on the v1.19.x backport).

signals.title: policy: Fix data race on the map state identity index
signals.text: Please ensure your pull request adheres to the following guidelines: - [x] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [x] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [x] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a `Fixes: #XXX` line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [x] If your commit description contains a `Fixes: <commit-id>` tag, then please add the commit author[s] as reviewer[s] to this issue. - [x] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer’s Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! --- cilium-agent dies with `fatal error: concurrent map iteration and map write` when an endpoint's policy is recomputed while incremental policy map changes are applied concurrently: ``` fatal error: concurrent map iteration and map write pkg/policy.newMapState pkg/policy/mapstate.go:731 pkg/policy.(*selectorPolicy).DistillPolicy pkg/policy/resolve.go:419 pkg/endpoint.(*Endpoint).regeneratePolicy pkg/endpoint/policy.go:275 ``` `DistillPolicy` deliberately runs with the endpoint unlocked so the ipcache can make progress, but it sized the new map state from the owner's *live* previous map state — `len()` on the entries map and, when the identity index (`byId`) is in use, iterating it for per-identity key counts — while `Endpoint.ApplyPolicyMapChanges` mutates those same maps under the endpoint lock. No lock is shared between the two. This became reachable on most endpoints under ordinary pod churn when the identity-index gate was widened from pass rules to named-port rules (d1c81b3a5624); before that it needed the rarely used pass rules. ### The fix, and why the interface changes shape `PolicyOwner.PreviousMapState() *MapState` becomes `PreviousMapStateSizes() MapStateSizes`, a value snapshot taken under the endpoint lock. The pointer-returning form was not a content-access contract. Before 1c4121caba5a the interface method was `MapStateSize() int` — a pure sizing hint. That commit widened it to the whole pointer only because the new `byId` index also needed per-identity keyset sizes, and the only consumer (`newMapState`, via `resolve.go`) has ever read just lengths from it: `len(old.entries)`, `len(old.byId)` and `len(v)` per keyset. One existing mock even returns nil. This restores the original sizing-accessor contract, generalized to carry the per-identity sizes the index needs, with the snapshot taken under the right lock. The accessor is called before the selector cache read lock is taken: the endpoint takes the selector cache write lock while holding its own lock (e.g. when `setDesiredPolicy` detaches a superseded policy), so taking the endpoint lock inside `WithRLock` would invert the established lock order and deadlock. Cost of the snapshot is O(#identities in the index): ~+175µs, +148KB, +18 allocs per `DistillPolicy` at a worst-case 4096-identity index, noise otherwise — microseconds against multi-millisecond regenerations. ### Backport Suggest backporting to v1.20: both `Fixes:` commits are in v1.20, so the crash is reachable there. The commit cherry-picks cleanly onto the current v1.20 head and the touched packages pass unit, `-race`, integration and privileged suites there. ### Follow-ups, deliberately not in this PR - The same race class remains in the `cilium-dbg policy` commands, which read live map state unlocked after `GetDesiredPolicy` returns: `pkg/policy/commands/topk.go:130` and `pkg/policy/commands/mapstate.go:73`. - The `rlockAlive`-error branch of the new accessor (disconnecting endpoint → zero sizes) has no dedicated test; a one-line companion test can follow. - Pre-existing breakage on main, unrelated but hit while validating: `TestComputeCIDRLabels` flakes under `-race` (leaked controller goroutine from `TestInitialNamedPortsIdentityLabel`); `BenchmarkRegenerateCIDRPolicyRules` (stale entry-count assert) and `BenchmarkEvaluateL4PolicyMapState/IncrementalToMapState` (index panic) both fail under `-bench`, which nothing in CI runs. Adding @jrajahalme as reviewer, as the author of both `Fixes:` commits. This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked the diff, the lock-order reasoning against the selector-cache and endpoint lock paths, the regression tests and their mutation checks, and the validation results below. Validation: five regression tests (race detector plus a deadlock watchdog), each mutation-checked; containerised unit, integration and privileged suites with no failures attributable to this branch; and a live cluster running a `-race` + go-deadlock agent image through ~2h of pod and policy churn with named-port policies active, with zero race, deadlock or crash reports. ```release-note Fixed a cilium-agent crash (`fatal error: concurrent map iteration and map write`) when an endpoint's policy was recomputed while incremental policy map changes were being applied concurrently. This was most commonly triggered by policies using named ports under pod churn. ``` [AI Influence Level]: https://danielmiessler.com/blog/ai-influence-level-ail [Cilium AI Policy]: https://github.com/cilium/community/blob/main/AI-POLICY.md [Developer’s Certificate of Origin]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#dev-coo [Submitting a pull request]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#submitting-a-pull-request

signals.title: node: Add NodeWriter and use it in NodeManager
signals.text: This introduces the `node.Writer` for controlled writes into the Table[Node]. On `Upsert` we check for conflicts with existing nodes. If a node exists with the same name, but different source then the highest priority source wins, and if a node exists with a different name that holds any of the addresses of the new node we check for source priority and if source is equal or higher the new node replaces the old node. As with NodeManager we don't set aside the losing nodes and restore them later. In other words, this aims to keep the same exact semantics as before. AIL:3 Related: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/41744

signals.title: node: Derive cluster-size intervals from table
signals.text: Provide a cluster-size-dependent interval function backed by the current number of objects in Table[*node.Node]. Use it for KVStore, ClusterMesh, and status intervals, removing the public NodeManager dependency while retaining the manager private calculation for its temporary background validation loop. signals.title: CLI: add toleration for a single etcd container restart
signals.text: Each pod is associated with a single `/etc/hosts` file that is mounted inside each container of the pod, and the kubelet enforces its content again every time that a container is started, through [os.WriteFile] [1]. However, this leaves a tiny race condition window in which an already started container may observe a truncated version of the hosts file. No race condition is small enough to escape our CI, and we witnessed the etcd container fail to resolve the localhost hostname when configuring the peer listeners, and exit [2], eventually tripping this restart check. Ideally, we'd not rely on a hostname there, but that's easier said than done, because a direct use of either 127.0.0.1 or [::1] would not work if the corresponding IP family is disabled. For the moment, let's tolerate a possible restart of this container. \[1]: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/65bca7cd12f0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L491-L515 \[2]: [...] "msg":"creating peer listener failed","error":"listen tcp: lookup localhost on 10.245.0.10:53: no such host" AIL: 0 for the creation of the patch (although I leveraged AI to help with the investigation of the flake)
