signal.title: daemon: fall back to API server when pod is missing from cache during restore
signal.text: During agent restarts or rolling updates, the pod informer cache can experience eventual consistency delays when pulling data from the API server's internal watch cache. This occasionally causes `getPodForEndpoint` to fail cache lookups for valid pods, skipping endpoint restoration. The orphaned endpoints are subsequently deleted by the `stale-endpoint-cleanup` routine. This commit prevents premature endpoint drops by modifying `getPodForEndpoint` to fall back to a direct Kubernetes API server query if a pod cache miss occurs. To enable testing of this workflow without spinning up a heavy daemon: - Converted `endpointRestorer.k8sWatcher` into a lightweight internal interface. - Added unit tests in `endpoint_restore_test.go` isolating the fallback logic. signal.title: bandwidth: support DSCP marking for Pod egress traffic
signal.text: This PR adds support for setting DSCP marks on Pod egress traffic through the Bandwidth Manager. Pods can configure the DSCP value with the `bandwidth.cilium.io/egress-dscp` annotation. The annotation accepts values in the `0-63` range. The BPF datapath preserves the existing ECN bits while rewriting the IPv4 TOS or IPv6 Traffic Class field. The feature is held behind `--enable-dscp-marking` / `bandwidthManager.dscp.enabled`, and requires the Bandwidth Manager to be enabled. Then annotate a Pod, e.g. for Expedited Forwarding (DSCP 46): ```yaml metadata: annotations: bandwidth.cilium.io/egress-dscp: "46" ``` Follow ups: - Tunnel outer-header DSCP marking is not included in this PR and will be covered separately. - User-facing documentation will be added in a follow-up PR. Refs: #43150 ```release-note Add support for setting DSCP marks on Pod egress traffic through the Bandwidth Manager using the `bandwidth.cilium.io/egress-dscp` annotation. ```

signal.title: fix(bgp): only auto-discover the default gateway from the main table
signal.text: - [x] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [x] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [x] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a Fixes: #XXX line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [x] If your commit description contains a Fixes: <commit-id> tag, then please add the commit author[s] as reviewer[s] to this issue. - [x] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer’s Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! BGP peer auto-discovery in defaultGateway mode walks the whole StateDB route table and picks the default route with the lowest metric. The route table is populated from a RT_TABLE_UNSPEC netlink dump, so it holds default routes from every table, not just main — and a default route outside main is not the way off the node. This matters in practice because Cilium installs one itself. With native routing plus any of EnableEnvoyConfig, IPsec, or WireGuard, installFromProxyRoutes* adds default via <cilium_host address> dev cilium_host to table 2005 (RouteTableFromProxy) with no metric, i.e. priority 0. That outranks a real uplink default route, which typically carries a non-zero metric, so auto-discovery hands BGP the cilium_host address as the peer address and the session never comes up. Table 2004 (RouteTableToProxy) similarly holds a local default dev lo; it has no nexthop so it was already skipped, but nothing made that intentional. Restrict selection to unicast routes in the main table, which is where the node's default gateway lives. Non-unicast types (local, blackhole, unreachable, prohibit) do not forward anything either. Test changes: - A new unit case models a node with a metric-1024 main-table default route alongside a metric-0 local default dev lo in table 2004 and a metric-0 default via 10.0.5.160 in table 2005, and asserts the main-table gateway still wins. Existing default routes are built through a small defaultRouteEntry helper so every fixture carries a realistic table and type. - peering-default-gateway.txtar now sets table: 254 / type: 1 on its routes. The fixture previously left both at zero (RT_TABLE_UNSPEC / RTN_UNSPEC), which the kernel never reports for an installed route. release-note Fix BGP `defaultGateway` peer auto-discovery selecting a default route from a non-main routing table, such as the `default via cilium_host` route Cilium installs in the from-proxy table, instead of the node's real default gateway. This PR was prepared with AIL:2. I personally wrote or checked all code and validated the behavior end-to-end against a live cluster and DPU as peer (on the v1.19.x backport).

signal.title: Gateway API: 503 connection timeout for same-node backends with L2 announcements and VXLAN tunnel mode
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.20.0 and lower than v1.21.0 ### What happened? Gateway API with L2 announcements and VXLAN tunnel mode produces 503 "upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers. reset reason: connection timeout" for **all backend pods running on the same node that holds the L2 VIP lease**. Backend pods on other nodes work perfectly. The pattern is deterministic and follows the L2 lease holder: - When `node-a` holds the lease: all backends on `node-a` return 503, all backends on other nodes return 200 - When the lease moves (e.g. after a cilium restart): the failures follow the lease to the new holder node Envoy admin cluster stats confirm the pattern. Cross-node connectivity from regular pods (both with and without hostNetwork) works fine - this is specific to the envoy TPROXY path. `proxy-use-original-source-address` is hardcoded to `true` by the Helm chart when `kubeProxyReplacement: true`, and cannot be overridden via Helm values. This might be the root cause: envoy connects to same-node pods using the external client's source IP via TPROXY, and the response packet from the backend pod cannot route back to envoy correctly in VXLAN tunnel mode. **Please note that I did this research with Claude. I haven't tested the workaround yet.** ### How can we reproduce the issue? **Environment:** 3-node k3s cluster on Raspberry Pi (arm64), Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0.0-1016-raspi **Cluster topology:** - `jarvis` (control-plane): 192.168.10.100, pod CIDR 10.0.1.0/24 - `node-a` (worker): 192.168.10.101, pod CIDR 10.0.2.0/24 - `node-b` (worker): 192.168.10.102, pod CIDR 10.0.0.0/24 **Steps:** 1. Install Cilium with the following Helm values: ```yaml kubeProxyReplacement: true gatewayAPI: enabled: true l2announcements: enabled: true l7Proxy: true bpf: tproxy: true devices: eth0 envoy: enabled: true securityContext: capabilities: envoy: - NET_ADMIN - SYS_ADMIN - NET_BIND_SERVICE keepCapNetBindService: true socketLB: enabled: true hostNamespaceOnly: false operator: replicas: 1 ``` 2. Create a CiliumLoadBalancerIPPool and CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy: ```yaml apiVersion: cilium.io/v2alpha1 kind: CiliumLoadBalancerIPPool metadata: name: gateway-lan-pool spec: blocks: - start: 192.168.10.50 stop: 192.168.10.50 --- apiVersion: cilium.io/v2alpha1 kind: CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy metadata: name: l2-announcement spec: interfaces: - ^eth0 loadBalancerIPs: true ``` 3. Create a Gateway with multiple HTTPS listeners and HTTPRoutes pointing to services on different nodes 4. Observe that backends on the node holding the L2 lease (check via `kubectl get leases -n kube-system | grep cilium-l2announce`) return 503, while backends on other nodes work **Verification commands:** ```bash # Check which node holds the lease kubectl get leases -n kube-system cilium-l2announce-default-cilium-gateway-http-gateway -o jsonpath='{.spec.holderIdentity}' # Check envoy cluster stats (run on the cilium pod of the lease-holding node) kubectl exec -n kube-system <cilium-pod> -- cilium-dbg envoy admin clusters | grep -E "(cx_connect_fail|rq_success|rq_error)" # Test cross-node connectivity from a regular pod (works fine) kubectl run tmp --rm -i --restart=Never --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://<backend-pod-ip>:<port> # Test from hostNetwork pod on the lease-holding node (also works fine) kubectl run tmp --rm -i --restart=Never --overrides='{"spec":{"hostNetwork":true,"nodeName":"<lease-holder>"}}' --image=curlimages/curl -- curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://<backend-pod-ip>:<port> ``` Both connectivity tests return 200, proving the issue is specific to the envoy TPROXY path, not general network connectivity. ### Relevant log output Curl response from the gateway for a same-node backend: ``` > GET / HTTP/1.1 > Host: argocd.jarvis-home.dev < HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable < content-length: 91 < content-type: text/plain < server: envoy upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers. reset reason: connection timeout ``` Envoy admin cluster stats for the failing backend (same node as lease holder): ``` argocd:argocd-server:80::10.0.2.4:8080::cx_active::0 argocd:argocd-server:80::10.0.2.4:8080::cx_connect_fail::14 argocd:argocd-server:80::10.0.2.4:8080::cx_total::14 argocd:argocd-server:80::10.0.2.4:8080::rq_active::0 argocd:argocd-server:80::10.0.2.4:8080::rq_error::14 argocd:argocd-server:80::10.0.2.4:8080::rq_success::0 argocd:argocd-server:80::10.0.2.4:8080::health_flags::healthy ``` Envoy admin cluster stats for a working backend (different node from lease holder): ``` technitium:technitium-svc:5380::10.0.1.131:5380::cx_active::6 technitium:technitium-svc:5380::10.0.1.131:5380::cx_connect_fail::0 technitium:technitium-svc:5380::10.0.1.131:5380::cx_total::14 technitium:technitium-svc:5380::10.0.1.131:5380::rq_active::0 technitium:technitium-svc:5380::10.0.1.131:5380::rq_error::0 technitium:technitium-svc:5380::10.0.1.131:5380::rq_success::67 technitium:technitium-svc:5380::10.0.1.131:5380::health_flags::healthy ``` Relevant cilium-config values: ``` routing-mode: tunnel tunnel-protocol: vxlan proxy-use-original-source-address: "true" enable-bpf-tproxy: "true" external-envoy-proxy: "true" kube-proxy-replacement: "true" gateway-api-hostnetwork-enabled: "false" bpf-lb-sock-hostns-only: "true" ``` ### Workaround Setting `proxy-use-original-source-address: "false"` in the cilium-config ConfigMap and restarting cilium + cilium-envoy DaemonSets resolves the issue. However, this cannot be done via Helm values because the chart hardcodes this to `true` when `kubeProxyReplacement: true`. ### Additional context - The issue was initially observed with technitium (DNS server) being the only pod on the control-plane node. When the L2 lease was on that node, only technitium failed. After a cilium restart moved the lease to a worker node, technitium started working but all worker-node backends broke. - `gatewayAPI.hostNetwork.enabled: true` has no effect when `external-envoy-proxy: true` (Cilium 1.20 default) - no dedicated gateway pods are created. - Related issues with similar symptoms but different root causes: #42325, #35559, #36004, #32592 ### Cilium Version 1.20.0 ### Kernel Version Linux drone-two 7.0.0-1016-raspi #16-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Thu Jul 23 22:56:44 UTC 2026 aarch64 GNU/Linux ### Kubernetes Version v1.36.3+k3s1 ### Regression _No response_ ### Sysdump [cilium-sysdump-20260818-144359.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31178210/cilium-sysdump-20260818-144359.zip) ### Relevant log output ```shell ``` ### Anything else? _No response_ ### Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? Please add yourself to the [Users doc](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/USERS.md) ### Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: operator: add --enable-unmanaged-pod-observe-only flag
signal.text: Please ensure your pull request adheres to the following guidelines: - [x] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [x] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [x] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a `Fixes: #XXX` line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [x] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer's Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. **AI Disclosure (AIL:3):** I identified the need for this mode, designed the flag and Helm integration, tested both modes on a live cluster, and validated the metric, RBAC, and log behaviour. An LLM (Claude) assisted with code authoring and test writing under my full review. ## Problem The `restart-unmanaged-pods` controller is all-or-nothing: it either detects and deletes unmanaged pods (active) or is fully disabled via `--unmanaged-pod-watcher-interval=0` (no detection, no metric, no deletions). There is no intermediate state where the controller runs purely for observability — counting unmanaged pods and emitting `cilium_operator_unmanaged_pods` — without issuing pod deletions. This becomes a problem when broadening `--pod-restart-selector` beyond the default `k8s-app=kube-dns` to cover more workloads: the moment the wider selector is deployed, the controller begins deleting matching pods with no observation window. Using `--unmanaged-pod-watcher-interval=0` as a workaround disables the entire controller, so the metric is never updated and the operator emits no signal at all. ## Fix Split into two commits: **Commit 1 — Go implementation:** Add `--enable-unmanaged-pod-observe-only` (default: `false`) to `cell.go`. Wire an `observeOnly` field through `unmanagedPodsController`. In `reconcile()`, add an observe-only branch that publishes `cilium_operator_unmanaged_pods` on every cycle but skips all `Pods().Delete()` calls. The branch still evaluates restart candidates (age + per-pod cooldown) to report how many pods *would* be restarted in the log, without acting. Setting `observeOnly=true` activates the controller even when `restart=false`. The flag uses `--enable-unmanaged-pod-observe-only` rather than the issue's proposed `--unmanaged-pod-restart-enabled` to follow Cilium's `--enable-X` convention and keep it additive by default. **Commit 2 — Helm and docs:** Add `operator.unmanagedPodWatcher.observeOnly: false` to the chart. The configmap template activates the watcher when `restart OR observeOnly` is true. The `pod/delete` ClusterRole permission is omitted when `observeOnly=true` since the controller never issues deletions in that mode. Update `helm-values.rst`, `k8s-install-migration.rst`, and regenerate all `Documentation/cmdref/` files. ## Testing **Unit tests** (`operator/unmanagedpods/controller_test.go`): - `TestReconcileObserveOnly` (table-driven) — gauge accuracy across varied pod populations; zero deletions in observe-only mode - `TestReconcileObserveOnlyRepeatable` — gauge stays accurate across repeated cycles, no restart cooldown recorded - `TestReconcileObserveOnlyLogsOnlyOnCountChange` — Info log fires on eligible-count change only, suppressed on steady-state cycles **Live cluster verification:** - `observeOnly=true`: metric increments on unmanaged pod detection, zero pod deletions confirmed, `pod/delete` permission absent from operator ClusterRole - `observeOnly=false` (default): pod deleted and metric drops to 0 as expected Fixes: #46198 ```release-note Add --enable-unmanaged-pod-observe-only flag to the Cilium operator. When enabled, the unmanaged pod watcher counts and reports unmanaged pods via the cilium_operator_unmanaged_pods metric without restarting (deleting) them, enabling safe phased rollouts when broadening --pod-restart-selector.

signal.title: bpf: Enable extended masquerade port range for BPF masquerade
signal.text: Under heavy outbound egress traffic, pods undergoing BPF masquerading can experience SNAT port exhaustion when restricted to the standard port range (`32768-65535`). This is a particular concern for users migrating from Kubernetes ip-masq-agent to Cilium eBPF masquerade, because the two have different default source port ranges: - Cilium eBPF masquerade selects any port in `32768-65535` by default. - Kubernetes ip-masq-agent selects any port in `1024-65535` by default. This change introduces support for configuring an extended masquerade port range (`--node-port-nat-range-ext`, e.g. `1024,29999`) across IPv4 and IPv6 to achieve source port range parity: 1. Refactor NAT Port Ranges into Runtime Config: - Replaced compile-time `#define NODEPORT_PORT_MIN/MAX_NAT` with dynamic BPF runtime config variables (`nodeport_port_min_nat` and `nodeport_port_max_nat`). 2. Extended Masquerade Port Range Support: - Added `--node-port-nat-range-ext` CLI flag in Hive loadbalancer configuration and mapped it to Helm. - Enforced validation rules (range bounds checking, ensuring non-overlap with NodePort range and privileged ports). - Implemented random port range selection in BPF for outgoing SNAT flows. - Added automatic fallback to the alternative range if the selected port range encounters allocation exhaustion. signal.title: helm: allow attachMetadata on the ServiceMonitors of host-network components
signal.text: ## Problem `cilium-agent`, `cilium-envoy`, `cilium-operator` and the Hubble metrics endpoint all run on the host network, so their scrape targets are node addresses. On a cluster where those node ports are not reachable from Prometheus — a closed node firewall, or nodes that are not mutually routable on the address kubelet reports — the only way to reach them is to rewrite `__address__` to an address Cilium itself publishes, such as the node's `cilium_host` address in `network.cilium.io/ipv{4,6}-cilium-host`. The chart already exposes `relabelings` for that. But a relabeling can only read labels service discovery produced, and node annotations are attached only when the ServiceMonitor sets `attachMetadata: {node: true}`. That field has no value in the chart, so the monitors cannot express it — which forces users to disable the chart's monitors entirely and hand-write equivalents outside it just to add one field. Concretely, this is what it takes today to scrape the agent on a cluster whose node ports are closed: ```yaml spec: attachMetadata: {node: true} # <- not expressible in the chart endpoints: - port: metrics relabelings: - action: replace sourceLabels: [__meta_kubernetes_node_annotation_network_cilium_io_ipv6_cilium_host] regex: (.+) replacement: "[$1]:9962" targetLabel: __address__ ``` ## Change Adds `attachMetadata` to the four `serviceMonitor` blocks whose targets are host-network, and renders it when set: - `prometheus.serviceMonitor.attachMetadata` - `operator.prometheus.serviceMonitor.attachMetadata` - `hubble.metrics.serviceMonitor.attachMetadata` - `envoy.prometheus.serviceMonitor.attachMetadata` `hubble-relay` and `clustermesh-apiserver` are deliberately not included — they are ordinary Deployments where node metadata has no use. Happy to extend for uniformity if reviewers prefer that. ## Verification - With the value set, all four ServiceMonitors render `spec.attachMetadata.node: true`. - With it unset (the default `{}`), the rendered chart is **byte-identical** to before the change. - README values table updated to match. ```release-note Added `attachMetadata` to the Helm ServiceMonitor values for cilium-agent, cilium-envoy, cilium-operator and Hubble metrics, so node labels and annotations can be used as relabeling sources when scraping these host-network components. ```

signal.title: allow cni channing generic veth to use bandwidth QoS
signal.text: ## Problem In CNI chaining mode (generic-veth, e.g. behind Kube-OVN), pod-ingress traffic is delivered to the pod veth directly by the chained CNI and reaches `cil_to_container`. It never traverses `local_delivery()`, which is the only place the ingress token-bucket policer (`accept()`) runs today. As a result, `kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth` QoS is silently not enforced for chained pods. ## Change - Apply the ingress bandwidth policer in `cil_to_container` for the generic-veth chaining case. The new site and the existing `local_delivery()` site are made mutually exclusive (gated on the chaining mode) so a packet is metered exactly once; otherwise a packet delivered via `local_delivery()` and then egressing the lxc device would be metered twice, halving the configured ingress rate. BPF host routing delivers via `redirect_peer()` and bypasses `cil_to_container`, hence the `!ENABLE_HOST_ROUTING` guard. - Convert `ENABLE_BANDWIDTH_MANAGER` from a compile-time `#define` into a node-level runtime config `CONFIG(enable_bandwidth_manager)`, in line with the ongoing migration of datapath configuration away from `#defines`. Its value is sourced from the bandwidth manager's post-probe state (`Manager.Enabled()`), threaded through the local node configuration like `EnableWireguard`/`EnableIPSec`, so it stays false when the manager disables itself (IPsec, unreadable procfs, …). Verifier/complexity coverage is preserved by exercising the toggle as a load-time permutation in `verifier_load_test.go`. ```release-note Enforce ingress bandwidth QoS (kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth) for pods using generic-veth CNI chaining. ``` # About AIL AIL:2 — I designed the feature and the datapath change; AI assistance was used for rebasing onto latest main, merge-conflict resolution, formatting cleanup and commit hygiene. I personally reviewed every change (bpf_lxc.c gating, edt.h/token_bucket.h runtime CONFIG conversion, Makefile/complexity-tests) and verified the build, BPF verifier permutations and unit tests locally.

I've been reviewing some cases where the cilium-agent is failing to startup happliy and goes into CLB for a while on new nodes in AWS. It appears that there can be some significant latency from when the `cilium-operator` calls `AtachNetworkInterface` to when that ENI actually shows up on the node from it's kernel logs. The worst case I've found over the last 2 weeks was 149 seconds. The compounding issue is that with the current max of 3.75s + kubelet's exponetial backoff restarting the agent, where in one case the NIC was there within 129-ish seconds but, the agent wasn't able to get through this until 212-ish seconds. Okay so, with the pre-ample out of the way, this PR drops the exponential backoff and switches to using PollUntilContextTimeout instead. immediate is passed as `true` so it checks right away, so any case where the NIC is there shouldn't see any backoff. Then it'll check every second up to 150 seconds. This changes the current checking behavior from something like `0.000 0.285 0.840 1.865 3.904` (with jitter, then gives up) to `0 1 2 3 4 5 ... 150` (fixed 1s, then gives up). No chart change is required. 150s fits inside both remaining ceilings: - cilium-agent `startupProbe: failureThreshold: 300` x `periodSeconds: 2` with `initialDelaySeconds: 5` == ~600s - https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/2efb257c8533af4a446af77813d9aaa9d8b127fc/install/kubernetes/cilium/values.yaml#L2428-L2433 - `defaults.HiveStartTimeout` = 300s - https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/pkg/defaults/defaults.go#L12-L13 ```release-note ipam: Wait up to 150s for attached ENI's to show up ``` Noting too that this is related to https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/47295 and the original PR https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/41954. Fixes: trafficDistribution hints on non-active backends ## Summary - This PR was prepared with AIL:2. I personally implemented fix in code, used AI for tests and better descriptions. - With `trafficDistribution: PreferSameNode` and a single node-local backend (e.g. a DaemonSet), restarting that local backend causes a multi-second window where an in-cluster client on the same node gets `connection refused` instead of falling back to a ready remote backend. - The drain side works correctly: while the old local Pod is `Terminating`, traffic falls back to remote backends. The drop happens only on the **return** side — while the replacement Pod is starting. During startup the replacement backend is programmed in `BackendStateMaintenance`, and `topologyPreferenceCandidate` does not exclude that state, so `PreferSameNode` treats it as a valid same-node candidate, commits to "same-node only", and pins traffic to a backend that cannot yet serve. - This is the startup-side analogue of the draining-side bug fixed for `Terminating` backends in #46339. That fix excluded `Terminating`/`TerminatingNotServing` (states 1/2); the candidate check still accepts `Quarantined` (3) and `Maintenance` (4), and a starting backend lands in `Maintenance` (4). ### Current behaviour - During drain of the old local Pod: requests fall back to a remote backend (correct, no drop). - While the replacement Pod is starting: `connection refused` for the whole starting window, instead of continued fallback to a remote backend. Recovery coincides with the new Pod becoming Ready. ### Expected - While the returning same-node backend is not yet serving, `PreferSameNode` should keep falling back to ready remote backends (as it already does during drain), then snap back to the local backend once it is serving. No connection-refused window. ## PR-implemented fix - Require `Active` state for topology-preference candidacy even for non-health-checked services. - This subsumes the existing terminating checks and also excludes `Maintenance`/`Quarantined`. signal.title: lbmap: display proxy port for L7 services
signal.text: ## lbmap: display proxy port for L7 services When dumping entries from `cilium_lb4_services_v2`, L7 service entries are currently displayed using the `BackendID` field. For L7 services, however, this field does not represent a backend ID. It stores the Envoy proxy port in network byte order. Since `Service4Value.String()` prints the raw field directly, the displayed value is byte-swapped on little-endian systems, making the output misleading. This PR detects L7 service entries via the `L7LB` service flag and displays the decoded proxy port instead, so that the output reflects the actual forwarding destination. ## Reproducer Create a Gateway API service backed by the Cilium L7 proxy. ```console $ kubectl get svc -n horizon-system cilium-gateway-horizon-gateway NAME TYPE CLUSTER-IP EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) cilium-gateway-horizon-gateway LoadBalancer 10.43.2.169 10.251.8.82 80:32201/TCP ``` The Envoy proxy allocated for this Gateway is listening on port `18036`: ```console $ netstat -anp | grep cilium-envoy | grep LISTEN tcp 0 0 127.0.0.1:18036 0.0.0.0:* LISTEN 2472775/cilium-envoy ``` The allocated proxy port is also recorded in Cilium's proxy state: ```console $ cat /var/run/cilium/state/proxy_ports_state.json { "horizon-system/cilium-gateway-horizon-gateway/listener": { "type": "crd", "ingress": false, "port": 18036 } } ``` However, dumping the service map shows: ```console $ cilium map get cilium_lb4_services_v2 | grep 10.251.8.82 10.251.8.82:80/TCP (0) 29766 0[0] (204) [0x60 0x4] ``` The value `29766` is not the actual proxy port. It is the raw network-byte-order representation of `18036` interpreted as a host-order integer. As a result, the output can be confusing when troubleshooting L7 load balancer entries. ## Root Cause For L7 service entries, the value stored in `BackendID` is actually the Envoy proxy port encoded in network byte order. `Service4Value.String()` always prints the raw `BackendID` field, so the proxy port is displayed incorrectly on little-endian architectures. ## Fix This PR updates `Service4Value.String()` to detect L7 service entries using the `L7LB` service flag. Instead of printing the raw `BackendID` field, it uses `GetL7LBProxyPort()` to decode the stored value into host byte order before formatting the output. ### Before ```console 10.251.8.82:80/TCP (0) 29766 0[0] (204) [0x60 0x4] ``` ### After ```console 10.251.8.82:80/TCP (0) 18036 0[0] (204) [0x60 0x4] ``` This change only affects the string representation used when dumping service map entries. It does not modify datapath behavior or the contents of the BPF maps.

signal.title: Persistent traffic drops after 1.18.10 → 1.19.5 upgrade - warning log "Skipping named port" for all named-port ingress rules
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.19.6 and lower than v1.20.0 ### What happened? During an in-place upgrade from 1.18.10 → 1.19.5, cilium pods were restarted as the Daemonset executed a `RollingUpdate`. One of the cilium-agent pods restarted with a bad state, causing all ingress traffic to be dropped for workloads on that node. The issue was only resolved after the pod was manually restarted. Upon upgrade, the problematic cilium-agent pod restarted and restored its existing endpoints (~18 endpoints total). During endpoint restore/regeneration, the agent: 1. Unpinned and recreated every per-endpoint policy map (`cilium_policy_v2_*`). I think this part is expected and benign because I see the `PolicyEntry` value struct changed between [`v1.18.10`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/v1.18.10/pkg/maps/policymap/policymap.go) and [`v1.19.5`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/v1.19.5/pkg/maps/policymap/policymap.go). 2. Emitted `Skipping named port` logs for the full set of named ports across all workload endpoints. ### Theory Regeneration logs reported success (`regenerated=18 failed=0`), but the named-port ingress allow rules were not programmed. The `Skipping named port` warnings were emitted once and regeneration was never retried, so the endpoints remained misconfigured. ### Additional context * The cluster uses a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy to implement a "default-deny" stance for all workloads in the namespace * Each workload defines its own CiliumNetworkPolicy to enable ingress and egress and those policies use L4 rules that reference named ports * [Policy enforcement](https://docs.cilium.io/en/latest/security/policy/intro/) is set to `default` mode ### How can we reproduce the issue? Unsure. It seems to be a race condition give that we saw this behavior on only 3 pods out of 1,800+ pods across various clusters. ### Cilium Version 1.19.5 ### Kernel Version 6.12.94-123.180.amzn2023.x86_64 ### Kubernetes Version 1.33 ### Regression Yes, this seems to be unique to the rule regeneration behavior for version 1.19. Our team cannot say we have definitely observed this problem during previous upgrades. ### Sysdump Not available. The affected `cilium-agent` pod was manually deleted to remediate the outage before a sysdump was captured. ### Relevant log output ```shell time=… level=info msg="Regenerating restored endpoints" module=agent.controlplane.endpoint-restore restored=18 time=… level=info msg="Unpinning map with incompatible properties" \ bpfMapPath=/sys/fs/bpf/tc/globals/cilium_policy_v2_0<ID> \ old="[type LPMTrie keySize 12 valueSize 8 maxEntries 32768 flags 1]" \ new="[type LPMTrie keySize 12 valueSize 12 maxEntries 32768 flags 129]" time=… level=warn msg="Skipping named port" \ ciliumEndpointName=<ns>/<pod> endpointID=<id> k8sPodName=<ns>/<pod> \ subsys=endpoint error="nil map" portName=broker protocol=TCP trafficDirection=ingress time=… level=info msg="Finished regenerating restored endpoints" \ module=agent.controlplane.endpoint-restore regenerated=18 failed=0 ``` ### Anything else? signal.title: hubble: Add Kubernetes Pod UID to flow endpoints
signal.text: Hubble currently identifies a Pod mainly by cluster, namespace, and name. Kubernetes permits a deleted object's name to be reused, while its UID identifies that specific object lifetime. This matters especially for StatefulSet Pods, but applies to any recreated Pod. Adding the UID improves flow attribution. Consumers can distinguish Pod instances and correlate flows with Kubernetes records keyed by UID. The UID is carried through IPCache and ClusterMesh metadata, so Hubble can expose it for remote endpoints when that metadata is available. Cilium also uses the UID internally: - IPCache deletion checks UID, preventing a delayed Pod, CEP, or CES deletion from removing metadata belonging to a replacement Pod. - Same-name Pod replacements update IPCache, cgroup, endpoint, and host-network state. IPCache and NOTRACK changes install new state before removing old state, allowing a short overlap instead of a gap. - Kubernetes drop events use the UID captured in the flow instead of resolving whichever Pod currently owns that namespace/name. The UID remains optional when metadata is unavailable or components are running mixed versions. This PR was prepared with AIL:4. Codex drafted the implementation and tests. I reviewed the code and changed the replacement handling. ```release-note Hubble flow endpoints now include the Kubernetes Pod UID. ```

signal.title: BPF masquerade drops IPv6 Router Solicitations and Advertisements on nodes whose masquerade address is a link-local
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version Observed on v1.19.4, but this is not a version-specific bug: the ICMPv6 punt list in `snat_v6_nat()` is byte-for-byte identical in v1.19.4, v1.19.6, v1.20.0 and `main`, so every supported release is affected. I picked the exact-version fields below over the dropdown for that reason rather than to skip the upgrade check. ### What happened? On a node whose only IPv6 address on the selected devices is a link-local, IPv6 Router Solicitations and Router Advertisements emitted by the node are dropped by BPF masquerade: ``` xx drop (Unsupported protocol for NAT masquerade, -1) flow 0x0 , file nodeport_egress.h:152, identity host->unknown: fe80::bae9:24ff:fe80:ebfe -> ff02::1 icmp RouterAdvertisement ``` The chain is: 1. When no selected device has a global IPv6 address, the best IPv6 fallback node address is the link-local itself. `fallbackAddresses.update()` ranks candidates by public-vs-private and scope and does not exclude link-locals, so `bpfMasqAddrs()` hands that link-local to the datapath as `nat_ipv6_masquerade`. 2. RS/RA are always sourced from a link-local, so `__snat_v6_needs_masquerade()` matches such a packet on its very first test — source equals the masquerade address — and answers `NAT_NEEDED`. 3. That leaves `snat_v6_nat()` nothing but the ICMPv6 type to go on: it only consults `snat_v6_nat_can_skip()` for TCP/UDP/SCTP. It punts echo replies, redirects and NS/NA to the stack and returns `DROP_NAT_UNSUPP_PROTO` for everything else, including RS and RA. Expected: RS/RA reach the wire untranslated. Neighbor Discovery is link-local by definition and must never be masqueraded — rewriting an RA's source would advertise the masquerade address as the router's link-local. RFC 4890 §4.4, which 5244b68c1468 ("bpf: Hande icmpv6 in host firewall") cites when it added the NS/NA punt, lists RS/RA in the same must-not-be-dropped group. I hit this doing BGP unnumbered peering, where the node emits RAs out a Cilium-managed native device and the FRR peer will not accept an unnumbered neighbor whose link-local it has not learned from those RAs — but nothing about the drop is specific to BGP; any RA sender on such a node is affected. ### How can we reproduce the issue? 1. Install Cilium with BPF masquerade and IPv6 enabled: `--set enableIPv6Masquerade=true --set bpf.masquerade=true --set ipv6.enabled=true` 2. Use a node where none of the selected devices has a global IPv6 address, only a link-local, so the chosen `nat_ipv6_masquerade` is that link-local. Confirm with `cilium-dbg statedb node-addresses` / the agent's masquerade address in `cilium-dbg status`. 3. Emit an RA out that device from the host netns (radvd, `zebra`, or a crafted packet). 4. `cilium-dbg monitor --type drop` shows the drop above. A BPF unit test reproduces it without a cluster; it ships with the fix as `bpf/tests/host_bpf_masq_linklocal.c` and sets `nat_ipv6_masquerade` to the node's link-local and sends an RA and an RS through the host egress program. ### Cilium Version ``` Client: 1.19.4 go version go1.25.10 linux/amd64 Daemon: 1.19.4 go version go1.25.10 linux/amd64 ``` This is a build off the v1.19.4 tag carrying my in-flight BGP-unnumbered patches from #47394. None of them touch the NAT code — `bpf/lib/nat.h` is stock v1.19.4 here. ### Kernel Version ``` Linux node1 6.17.9-45-g435a44e1-coreweave-amd64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Thu Apr 9 14:24:27 UTC 2026 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux ``` ### Kubernetes Version ``` Client Version: v1.36.3 Kustomize Version: v5.8.1 Server Version: v1.35.4 ``` ### Regression Not a regression — the ICMPv6 punt list in `snat_v6_nat()` has never included RS/RA. It was added for NS/NA in 5244b68c1468. ### Anything else? A fix is on the way; it is being split out of #47394 into its own PR, which I will link here.

signal.title: Host firewall: policy-selected node is permanently isolated after reboot — host endpoint policy map ends up deny-all (cold boot, audit-off flip) or allow-all (runtime label add), never the computed policy
signal.text: ## Is there an existing issue for this? Closest match is #25448 ("host firewall drops reply traffic for legitimate connections when policies are first enforced"). This report is a stronger manifestation of what looks like the same enforcement-transition problem: in our setup the drop window is not transient — it is fatal and self-sustaining (node permanently isolated until out-of-band reboot), it reproduces on every cold boot, and it also reproduces on a fully synced agent when audit mode is switched off at runtime. Filing separately because the evidence points at the host endpoint's BPF policy map never receiving the computed allow entries, with three distinct end states depending on the path taken. ## What happened? Environment: Cilium 1.18.6 (kubespray), host firewall enabled, kube-proxy replacement enabled, VXLAN tunnel, WireGuard node encryption, `bpf-datapath-mode: netkit`, CRD identity mode, 61 nodes. A `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` with `nodeSelector` on worker nodes provides ingress lock-down (fromEntities cluster/remote-node/health/host, SSH/ICMP via CiliumCIDRGroup refs plus literal CIDRs, kubelet/NodePort from cluster). **1. Cold boot of a selected node → permanent isolation.** ~13 s after cilium-agent starts, every packet in and out is dropped as `Policy denied` by `bpf_host.c:865`. The node never recovers: the agent needs the apiserver to finish its sync, and its own egress to the apiserver is what is being dropped. Captured from inside a locked node (systemd unit dumping via crictl exec): - at agent start, `cilium-dbg endpoint list` is still **empty** (host endpoint not created yet) while bpf_host is already attached and enforcing deny-by-default with an empty policy map; - 105 659 `Policy denied` drops in 20 s, 73 018 of them the node's own egress to the apiserver LB: `identity host->unknown: <node-ip>:* -> <apiserver-lb-ip>:6443`; - at that moment the BPF ipcache is fully populated (8 292 entries) and local CIDR identities for the policy's allowed CIDRs are already allocated — e.g. ICMP from an explicitly allowed CIDR is dropped with its allocated identity (`identity 16777222->unknown`). The policy is computed; its allow entries are just not in the host endpoint policy map. **2. Runtime audit-off flip on a fully synced agent → same isolation.** Boot the node with `policy-audit-mode: true` (per-node CiliumNodeConfig): node comes up healthy, host endpoint reaches `state=ready`, realized policy has all 8 L4 ingress rules, `enforcement=audit-ingress`. Then `cilium-dbg endpoint config <hostep> PolicyAuditMode=Disabled` → "configuration updated successfully" → the node is fully isolated within seconds. The agent log ends abruptly mid incremental `UpdatePolicyMaps` processing with no error line — consistent with the deny default being installed while the allow entries never land. **3. Warm enforcement via label add → policy map silently allow-all.** With the agent fully synced and the node label added at runtime (CCNP starts selecting the node), the endpoint reports `enforcement=ingress`, but `cilium-dbg bpf policy get <hostep>` contains only the wildcard pair (`Allow Ingress ANY` prefix 0 / `Allow Egress ANY` prefix 0) — i.e. no actual enforcement. This is the only transition that leaves the node reachable, and it appears to do so by not programming the policy at all. For contrast, a long-running node whose agent processed the CCNP incrementally while already enforcing has a fully programmed map (per-identity allows, port ranges) — so the policy→map pipeline itself works. So the same policy, same version, produces three different host endpoint policy-map end states depending on the transition path: deny-all (cold boot, audit-off flip), allow-all (runtime label add), correct (incremental update on an already-enforcing endpoint). Datapath mode does not appear to matter: a cold boot with `bpf-datapath-mode: veth` (per-node CiliumNodeConfig) locked out identically (caveat: the override's application could not be positively confirmed from inside the locked node). Impact: any reboot of a policy-selected node isolates it permanently; recovery requires out-of-band console/rescue access. 54 nodes affected in our cluster. ## Cilium Version 1.18.6 ## Kernel Version 6.8.0-124-generic (Ubuntu 24.04) ## Kubernetes Version v1.33.7 (kubespray) ## Sysdump Not attached (production cluster); can provide targeted captures on request. Full monitor drop capture (17 MB) and repeated boot-time snapshots of `endpoint list` / `bpf policy get` / `bpf ipcache list` from inside a locked node are preserved. ## Relevant log output ``` xx drop (Policy denied) flow 0x... to endpoint 0, ifindex 7, file bpf_host.c:865, , identity host->unknown: <node-ip>:39186 -> <apiserver-lb-ip>:6443 tcp SYN xx drop (Policy denied) flow 0x... to endpoint 0, ifindex 2, file bpf_host.c:865, , identity 16777222->unknown: <allowed-admin-ip> -> <node-ip> icmp EchoRequest ``` Agent start with audit mode (the boot that survives): ``` level=warn msg="PolicyAuditMode is enabled. Network policy will not be enforced." level=info msg="Regenerating restored endpoints" restored=0 level=info msg="Creating host endpoint" ``` ## Anything else? - The reboot lockout window matches #25448's "first enforcement" semantics; unlike #25448 the state is permanent because the dropped traffic includes the agent's own apiserver path (chicken-and-egg). - Feature combination overlaps with #31209 (tunnel + KPR + WireGuard + host firewall). - Nothing relevant found in 1.18.7–1.18.13 changelogs. - Happy to run instrumented builds / additional captures on a dedicated test node. ## Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: NetworkPolicy silently not enforced for pods carrying a label with key `host` (v1.20.0)
signal.text: ## Summary A Kubernetes pod carrying a label whose **key** is `host` has **all NetworkPolicy enforcement silently disabled**. The pod is not isolated and nothing anywhere reports a problem. The label's *value* is irrelevant. This is security-relevant: a workload that happens to use a `host` label (e.g. `host: <nodename>`, a common convention for pinning/labelling probes) silently loses its network isolation while passing every health check. ## Steps to reproduce Two pods that are identical except that one carries an extra `host` label, and two identical NetworkPolicies, each selecting its own pod by its `app` label: ```yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: {name: lblbug} --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: {name: p-a, namespace: lblbug, labels: {app: p-a}} spec: containers: - {name: c, image: "registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.47", args: ["netexec","--http-port=8080"]} --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: {name: p-b, namespace: lblbug, labels: {app: p-b, host: anything}} spec: containers: - {name: c, image: "registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.47", args: ["netexec","--http-port=8080"]} --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: {name: cli, namespace: lblbug, labels: {app: cli}} spec: containers: - {name: c, image: "registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/agnhost:2.47", command: ["sleep","infinity"]} --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: {name: iso-a, namespace: lblbug} spec: podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: p-a}} policyTypes: [Ingress] ingress: [{from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: nope}}}]}] --- apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: NetworkPolicy metadata: {name: iso-b, namespace: lblbug} spec: podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: p-b}} policyTypes: [Ingress] ingress: [{from: [{podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: nope}}}]}] ``` Then, from `cli`, reach each target on port 8080. **Expected:** both `p-a` and `p-b` are blocked — each is selected by a policy whose only ingress rule matches a label that exists on nothing. **Actual:** ``` p-a {app: p-a} -> BLOCKED (correct) p-b {app: p-b, host: anything} -> REACHABLE (policy not enforced) ``` ## Evidence `cilium-dbg endpoint list` on the node hosting both pods: ``` ENDPOINT POLICY (ingress) POLICY (egress) IDENTITY LABELS 1867 Enabled Disabled 12065 k8s:app=p-a 977 Disabled Disabled 7085 k8s:app=p-b ``` Everything upstream of enforcement looks correct for `p-b`: * the NetworkPolicy object is accepted; the agent logs `NetworkPolicy successfully added` * `cilium-dbg policy get` renders the rule correctly (`Tier: 200`, `"DefaultDeny": true`, `"Ingress": true`) * `cilium-dbg policy subject-selectors` resolves the rule's subject to **exactly that pod's identity**, `USERS=1` * the endpoint reaches the agent's current policy revision, state `ready`, no failing controllers Only `cilium-dbg statedb` (table `policy-computations`) dissents — and it reports **no error**: ``` Identity=12065 (p-a) IngressPolicyEnabled=true rev=2 ingressPortRules=256 Identity= 7085 (p-b) IngressPolicyEnabled=false rev=2 ingressPortRules=1 Err=null ``` The endpoint's BPF policy map for `p-b` holds a catch-all `Allow Ingress ANY`. ## Scope — only `host` One pod per candidate key, each with its own identical policy, all on the same node and namespace: ``` (no extra label) -> BLOCKED (enforced) host -> REACHABLE ** only failure ** world -> BLOCKED (enforced) health -> BLOCKED (enforced) init -> BLOCKED (enforced) remote-node -> BLOCKED (enforced) kube-apiserver -> BLOCKED (enforced) ``` So it is not reserved words generally — it is `host` specifically. ## Why this is easy to misdiagnose `PolicyEnforcement=always` is **also inert** on such a pod. Since `always` is defined to enforce default-deny on every endpoint irrespective of any rule, its failure reads as a broken cluster rather than a bad label — which is how we originally diagnosed it. It is consistent with the endpoint being treated as host-ish somewhere, given the host endpoint is exempt from policy unless the host firewall is enabled (`Host firewall: Disabled` here). This also means the usual checks all pass: the object exists, the agent logged success, translation is right, and the selector resolves to the right identity. signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version Cilium 1.17.3 ### What happened? When Cilium Socket-LB is enabled, NGINX connected UDP DNS sockets may be rewritten from the Kubernetes DNS Service IP to a CoreDNS Pod IP. Initially, after CoreDNS Pods were restarted and received new IP addresses, some existing NGINX UDP sockets continued to show the old CoreDNS Pod IP. During this period, NGINX DNS resolution could fail until NGINX was reloaded. However, the issue is intermittent and is no longer reproducible after reloading NGINX. After running: ```bash nginx -s reload subsequent CoreDNS Pod IP changes are handled correctly. Cilium Socket-LB removes the old backend IP, and newly created sockets use the current CoreDNS backend. ## Observed Result Before the NGINX reload, stale backend IPs were observed intermittently. After the NGINX reload: - The issue could no longer be reproduced. - Cilium Socket-LB cleaned up the old CoreDNS backend IP. - Newly created NGINX sockets used the current CoreDNS backend. - DNS resolution continued to work after subsequent CoreDNS Pod IP changes. ## Expected Behavior Cilium should clean up or re-evaluate connected UDP sockets when a CoreDNS backend Pod is deleted, without requiring an NGINX reload. The behavior should be consistent regardless of whether NGINX has recently been reloaded. ### How can we reproduce the issue? ## Reproduction Steps 1. Run NGINX for an extended period so that connected UDP DNS sockets are created. 2. Check the sockets: ss -up The peer may show a CoreDNS Pod IP instead of the DNS Service IP: <NGINX_POD_IP>:<SOURCE_PORT> -> <OLD_COREDNS_POD_IP>:53 3. NGINX reported errors similar to: could not be resolved (5: Operation refused) 8. Reload NGINX: nginx -s reload 9. signal.title: install: detect GKE from kubelet path
signal.text: GKE `1.36.2-gke.2064000` no longer exposes the container runtime endpoint through the `--container-runtime-endpoint` flag in `/etc/default/kubelet`. This causes the existing node-init GKE detection to miss the GKE-specific path and fall through to generic kubelet handling. Instead of detecting individual GKE node layouts through container runtime configuration, this change uses the presence of `/home/kubernetes/bin/kubelet`, which is shared by both the legacy and current GKE layouts. The same detection is used by startup and prestop, so the kubelet wrapper installed during startup can also be detected and reverted correctly. Testing performed: * `helm lint` * Helm template rendering with GKE/node-init values * `bash -n` on rendered startup and prestop scripts * sandboxed scenarios covering legacy GKE, the GKE 1.36.2 layout, generic non-GKE nodes, and an already-installed kubelet wrapper * live GKE `1.36.2-gke.2064000` COS/containerd node verification: * `/home/kubernetes/bin/kubelet` exists as a regular executable file * `/home/kubernetes/kubelet-config.yaml` contains `containerRuntimeEndpoint: unix:///run/containerd/containerd.sock` * `/etc/default/kubelet` does not contain `--container-runtime-endpoint` * `git diff --check` Claude was used to suggest the implementation. I manually reviewed the changes and validated the resulting behavior with the tests above. AIL:4 Fixes: #47884 ```release-note Fix node-init startup on GKE 1.36.2-gke.2064000 nodes by detecting GKE from the kubelet path instead of container runtime configuration. ```

signal.title: CFP: BFD(Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) support in BGP Control plane
signal.text: ## BFD(Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) support in BGP Control plane BFD is a health checking mechanism made for rapid (sub second) failure detection of data forwarding planes. Its a protocol which can be employed together with protocols such as BGP, IS-IS and OSFP to shorten the time between a failure and automated actions like retracting routes to reroute traffic. The protocol is describes in [RFC5880](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5880) with the addition of [RFC5881](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5881) for single hop and [RFC5882](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5882) for multi hop monitoring. Adding this feature to our BGP Control Plane would allow users with peers that also support the protocol to reduce downtime in case of failures in Cilium or between Cilium and peers. ## Implementation proposal Currently our only BGP backend is GoBGP which as of writing this has no BFD support. So we will have to implement it one way or another. ### GoBGP native The first logical approach would be to add it to GoBGP directly via a PR. GoBGP maintainers have already [indicated](https://github.com/osrg/gobgp/issues/2563) that they are open to PRs for this feature. Once BFD support is merged upstream and we are able to update to a GoBGP version with BFD support we will have to plumb access to it from our CRD. ### Cilium native The second approach would be to add BFD capabilities to Cilium directly, either in the agent or the datapath or a combination of the two. BFD works for any application where forwarding takes place such as the Cilium datapath. Having a non-BGP specific implementation would allow us to also use the protocol internally to monitor inter-node connections and connections in standalone L4LB for upstream and downstream. BFD control packets are sent over UDP in small packets (for IPv4/IPv6 single and multi hop) which is easily parse-able in both XDP and TC layers. The largest obstacle to a pure eBPF based implementation would be the need to send packets on a timer. However, if the peer is in Demand mode we only have to answer to Poll messages and optionally send echo messages back both of which are request-reply without delay. In this case, we should manually set associated BGP sessions to AdminDown in case of a BFD failure. ### CRD plubing No matter which route we take for BFD implementation, we will have to provide our users with a way to configure it. Since BGP Control Plane is backend agnostic and not all backends might implement BFD in future, I suggest adding a annotation for the top level CRD. Something like `io.cilium/bfd: "enabled=true,active=true,echo=false,detect-multiplied=5,receive-interval=40000,transmit-interval=20000"` ### User feedback Any information we have regrading BFD sessions should be added to the agent output (#22009). BFD adds additional diagnostic codes to communicate why a session is down which might be useful in figuring out what is going on. We should also add BFD specific information to the peer information to show the received discriminator and timing values. ### Metrics As soon as we have BFD session information, it should be added to the BGP metrics described in (#22010)

signal.title: fix(bpf): don't drop IPv6 RS/RAs when masquerading
signal.text: Please ensure your pull request adheres to the following guidelines: - [x] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [x] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [x] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a `Fixes: #XXX` line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [ ] If your commit description contains a `Fixes: <commit-id>` tag, then please add the commit author[s] as reviewer[s] to this issue. - [x] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer’s Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! `snat_v6_nat()` punts ICMPv6 echo replies, redirects and NS/NA to the stack but returns `DROP_NAT_UNSUPP_PROTO` for every other type, so Router Solicitations and Advertisements do not survive the egress masquerade path: ``` xx drop (Unsupported protocol for NAT masquerade, -1) flow 0x0 , file nodeport_egress.h:152, identity host->unknown: fe80::bae9:24ff:fe80:ebfe -> ff02::1 icmp RouterAdvertisement ``` This hits a node whose only IPv6 address is a link-local. RS/RA are always sourced from a link-local, and when no selected device has a global IPv6 address the best IPv6 fallback node address is the link-local itself — `fallbackAddresses.update()` ranks candidates by public-vs-private and scope, and does not exclude link-locals — so `bpfMasqAddrs()` hands that address to the datapath as `nat_ipv6_masquerade`. `__snat_v6_needs_masquerade()` then matches such a packet on its very first test, source equals the masquerade address, and answers `NAT_NEEDED`. That leaves `snat_v6_nat()` nothing but the ICMPv6 type to go on: it only consults `snat_v6_nat_can_skip()` for TCP/UDP/SCTP. Neighbor Discovery is link-local by definition and must never be masqueraded — rewriting an RA's source would advertise the masquerade address as the router's link-local. RFC 4890 section 4.4, which 5244b68c1468 ("bpf: Hande icmpv6 in host firewall") cites when it added the NS/NA punt, lists RS/RA in the same must-not-be-dropped group. Punt them to the stack alongside NS/NA, and cover both types with a BPF masquerade test for a node whose masquerade address is a link-local. Split out of #47394 so it can be reviewed and merged on its own; it is a standalone datapath fix that does not depend on the rest of that series. Fixes: #48093 ```release-note Fix IPv6 Router Solicitations and Router Advertisements being dropped with "Unsupported protocol for NAT masquerade" on nodes whose BPF masquerade address is a link-local address. ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:2. I personally wrote or checked all code and validated the behavior end-to-end against a live cluster and DPU (on the v1.19.x backport).

signal.title: Gateway-api: add support for session persistence
signal.text: Add cookie-based Gateway API session persistence for HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute rules as described in [CFP-47089](https://github.com/cilium/design-cfps/pull/102). Supported session persistence options are validated, with unsupported values being rejected. Accepted routes are ingested into the internal model and translated into CiliumEnvoyConfig. If a Gateway has any attached route rule containing a session persistence config, the Envoy stateful session filter is applied, alongside per-route cookie settings. Any routes attached to the Gateway without session persistence will explicitly disable the stateful session filter. The following HTTPRoute enables persistence for `/persistent`, while `/not-persistent` continues to use normal load balancing: ```yaml apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: HTTPRoute metadata: name: example-route spec: parentRefs: - name: example-gateway rules: - matches: - path: type: PathPrefix value: /persistent backendRefs: - name: example-service port: 8080 sessionPersistence: type: Cookie sessionName: app-session cookieConfig: lifetimeType: Session - matches: - path: type: PathPrefix value: /not-persistent backendRefs: - name: example-service port: 8080 ``` ```release-note Add support for Gateway API session persistence ``` AIL 2: Used to assist in planning, review, and generating some test cases.

signal.title: docs: note on eBPF ClusterIP translation vs Docker raw-table protection
signal.text: Document an interaction between Cilium's eBPF ClusterIP translation and Docker's raw-table protection that can affect hybrid Docker/Kubernetes hosts using unpublished Docker container backends. On such hosts, a `Service` backed by an unpublished Docker container can become unreachable from pods: Cilium translates the ClusterIP in the eBPF datapath, so the packet reaches Docker's `raw/PREROUTING` protection already addressed to the backend and is dropped before `DOCKER-USER`. This adds a short note to the kube-proxy-free documentation, next to the paragraph on per-packet ClusterIP load-balancing, together with a counter-based way to confirm the behaviour. Discussed and requested by a maintainer in #47601. Fixes: #47601 AI disclosure: AIL:2. Generative AI tools were used for research and technical analysis, and provided an initial draft which the author rewrote in their own words. The author independently reproduced and verified the described behaviour and takes full responsibility for the final content. ```release-note NONE ```

signal.title: mac: Make `mac.MAC` a `[6]byte`
signal.text: This PR migrates `pkg/mac.MAC` from being a [`net.HardwareAddr`](https://pkg.go.dev/net#HardwareAddr) (which is a `[]byte`) to being a `[6]byte`. Why we can do this: `net.HardwareAddr` has to be a slice because it has to support MAC address representations under different formats/size, such as the 20-octet IP over InfiniBand link-layer one. Cilium has always been stricter in the MAC addresses it accepts and already enforced the IEEE 802 MAC-48 format (see `mac.MAC`'s existing docstring: "MAC address is an net.HardwareAddr encapsulation to force cilium to only use MAC-48.") What we gain from doing this: We already wanted MAC-48-only format before, now this is guaranteed and enforced by the type itself, meaning we don't need to validate the value in as many places because once we have a valid `mac.MAC`, we know it's a 48 MAC. Switching from a slice to an array also means `MAC` becomes comparable (`m1 == m2`) and can be used as map keys (`map[mac.MAC]string` for example). From a memory point of view, an array is also better than a slice, but at this scale, the gain is probably not measurable. Overall, `[6]byte` is to `net.HardwareAddr` what `netip.Addr`/`netip.Prefix` are to `net.IP`/`net.IPNet`.

signal.title: CLI: add toleration for a single etcd container restart
signal.text: Each pod is associated with a single `/etc/hosts` file that is mounted inside each container of the pod, and the kubelet enforces its content again every time that a container is started, through [os.WriteFile] [1]. However, this leaves a tiny race condition window in which an already started container may observe a truncated version of the hosts file. No race condition is small enough to escape our CI, and we witnessed the etcd container fail to resolve the localhost hostname when configuring the peer listeners, and exit [2], eventually tripping this restart check. Ideally, we'd not rely on a hostname there, but that's easier said than done, because a direct use of either 127.0.0.1 or [::1] would not work if the corresponding IP family is disabled. For the moment, let's tolerate a possible restart of this container. \[1]: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/65bca7cd12f0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_pods.go#L491-L515 \[2]: [...] "msg":"creating peer listener failed","error":"listen tcp: lookup localhost on 10.245.0.10:53: no such host" AIL: 0 for the creation of the patch (although I leveraged AI to help with the investigation of the flake)

signal.title: policy: fix wildcard CIDR selector to match host/remote-node under policyCIDRMatchMode=nodes
signal.text: ## Problem \`matchesCIDRWildcard()\` in \`pkg/policy/types/selector.go\` only checked \`option.Config.PolicyCIDRMatchesPods()\` when deciding whether a wildcard CIDR requirement (e.g. one produced from a \`0.0.0.0/0\` \`CIDRRule\`) matches a target's labels. It never checked \`PolicyCIDRMatchesNodes()\`. As a result, when \`policyCIDRMatchMode\` is set to \`nodes\` (or \`nodes,pods\`) instead of the default \`pods\`, a \`0.0.0.0/0\` egress/ingress CIDR selector would **never** match \`host\`/\`remote-node\` identities, even though \`resolveLabels()\` (in \`pkg/ipcache/metadata.go\`) does attach a CIDR label to those identities under that same configuration. The selector's wildcard-matching short-circuit and the label-attachment logic had fallen out of sync. ### Impact This breaks connectivity to any host-networked destination (kube-apiserver, apiserver-proxy, etc.) reachable only via a wildcard CIDR egress rule, whenever an operator enables \`policyCIDRMatchMode=nodes\`. We observed this concretely on OpenShift 4.22 (HyperShift-hosted clusters), where CoreDNS's egress traffic to the API server was dropped with \`Policy denied\` (`bpf_lxc.c`, drop reason \`Policy denied\`), so DNS never stabilized despite CoreDNS actually being healthy — see #48034 for the full write-up including live \`cilium-dbg monitor --type drop\` captures showing this exact failure signature. ## Fix Extend \`matchesCIDRWildcard()\` to also permit a match when the target carries the \`host\` or \`remote-node\` reserved label **and** \`PolicyCIDRMatchesNodes()\` is enabled — mirroring exactly the condition used in \`resolveLabels()\` to decide whether to attach a CIDR label to that target in the first place. ## Testing - Added two new table-driven cases to \`TestCIDRRuleToCIDRSelectors\` in \`pkg/policy/types/selector_test.go\` covering: a wildcard CIDR rule matching \`host\`/\`remote-node\` when \`policyCIDRMatchesNodes\` is enabled, and *not* matching them when disabled (existing \`pods\`-only behavior is unchanged). - Live-validated end-to-end against a real OCP 4.22 HyperShift cluster (ARO-HCP) with custom-built agent+operator images including this fix: Cilium came up healthy, all default cluster operators (network, dns, ingress, etc.) reported Available, and no \`Policy denied\` drops were observed on CoreDNS→apiserver traffic — confirming the root cause and the fix. Fixes #48034

signal.title: node: Add NodeWriter and use it in NodeManager
signal.text: This introduces the `node.Writer` for controlled writes into the Table[Node]. On `Upsert` we check for conflicts with existing nodes. If a node exists with the same name, but different source then the highest priority source wins, and if a node exists with a different name that holds any of the addresses of the new node we check for source priority and if source is equal or higher the new node replaces the old node. As with NodeManager we don't set aside the losing nodes and restore them later. In other words, this aims to keep the same exact semantics as before. AIL:3 Related: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/41744

signal.title: cilium-cli/connectivity: detect Cilium version in connectivity perf setup
signal.text: `cilium connectivity perf` always reports "Cilium version: 0.0.0" in its info banner, regardless of the actual Cilium version running in the cluster. `setupAndValidatePerf()`, the setup path used by the `perf` subcommand, never calls `initCiliumPods()`/`detectCiliumVersion()`, unlike `setupAndValidate()` (used by `connectivity test`). `CiliumVersion` is therefore left at its Go zero value, which prints as `0.0.0`. This calls the same two steps `setupAndValidate()` already uses, in the same order, so `CiliumVersion` is populated before it's printed in `connectivity.Run()`. Tested manually against an RKE2 cluster (Cilium v1.19.4): - before the fix, `cilium connectivity perf` reported "Cilium version: 0.0.0" - after the fix, it correctly reports "Cilium version: 1.19.4" ```release-note Fixed `cilium connectivity perf` always reporting `Cilium version: 0.0.0` instead of the actual detected Cilium version.

signal.title: gateway-api: add support for ExtensionRef using Envoy ext_proc filter
signal.text: Add support for Gateway API `ExtensionRef` filters backed by a new typed `CiliumEnvoyExtProcFilter` CRD. This lets HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute attach Envoy `ext_proc` filters without requiring users to author raw `CiliumEnvoyConfig`. This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally reviewed each line of the submission. In addition to the Cilium Makefile validations, I ran tests in a live kind cluster that can be found here: https://github.com/eufriction/k8s-cilium-gapi#test-results-by-version. The implementation currently includes: - a namespaced `CiliumEnvoyExtProcFilter` - Gateway API ingestion and translation support for HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute `ExtensionRef` filters - feature-falgs for Helm and operator - ReferenceGrant enforcement and route status reporting for cross-namespace ext_proc backends - Envoy ext_proc metrics - unit/golden-file coverage plus user-facing documentation and examples. Design notes: - Envoy `ext_proc` filters are inserted before `ext_autz`. - I think the best long-term solution is to have a placement strategy with support for First, BeforeAuth, AfterAuth, and Last. This will not be included in this PR until more feedback from the community arrives as @youngnick suggest. - For this PR, Cilium resolves the order using Gateway API precedence: oldest route creation timestamp wins, followed by namespace/name and filter index. - Surfacing conflicts through a Gateway API status condition is not done yet. Could maybe wait for #46681? - Unresolved or invalid ext_proc BackendRefs fail closed. The affected route receives a configuration error and a 500 DirectResponse Fixes: #45951 ```release-note Gateway API HTTPRoute and GRPCRoute filters can reference CiliumEnvoyExtProcFilter resources via ExtensionRef to configure Envoy ext_proc filters. ```

signal.title: l2announcer: leader-election Lease name is a plain namespace+name concatenation, so two Services can end up sharing one Lease
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.19.6 and lower than v1.20.0 ### What happened? L2 announcements derive the per-Service leader-election Lease name by gluing the namespace and the Service name onto a prefix with a hyphen, and a hyphen is legal inside both halves. Two unrelated Services can therefore map onto the same Lease name and end up in one leader election. ```go const leasePrefix = "cilium-l2announce" Name: fmt.Sprintf("%s-%s-%s", leasePrefix, svc.Name.Namespace(), svc.Name.Name()), ``` https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/ee26050851a92746155a7319b2554054adb0966c/pkg/l2announcer/l2announcer.go#L847-L860 Namespace `foo` + Service `bar-baz`, and namespace `foo-bar` + Service `baz`, both produce `cilium-l2announce-foo-bar-baz`. There is no sanitization, escaping or hashing anywhere on that path; the only other place the name is touched is the GC scan, which just prefix-matches (`strings.HasPrefix(lease.Name, leasePrefix)`) and does not disambiguate either. Same code on v1.19: https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/44d55ea770e38bdf4b3a5f5d8079ab311f5a4911/pkg/l2announcer/l2announcer.go#L820-L826 Expected: one Lease per Service. ### Mechanism ### Impact Needs a hyphen in the right place, so it is not going to be common, but it is silent when it happens and the symptom points at the L2 policy rather than at a name collision. Multi-tenant clusters where namespaces are generated with a prefix (`team-a`, `team-a-staging`) and Service names are equally hyphenated are where I would expect it. ### Suggested fix Use a separator that cannot appear in either half. Neither a namespace (DNS-1123 label) nor a Service name (DNS-1035 label) may contain `.`, and `.` is legal in an object name (DNS-1123 subdomain), so `fmt.Sprintf("%s-%s.%s", leasePrefix, ns, name)` is unambiguous and stays readable in `kubectl get leases`. A hash suffix would also work but costs readability. Either way the name changes on upgrade, which orphans the existing Leases. Those are released on agent shutdown (`ReleaseOnCancel`), which empties the holder identity, and `leaseGC` already deletes prefix-matching Leases with an empty holder, so the old objects should clean themselves up. I have not confirmed that. ### How can we reproduce the issue? 1. Enable L2 announcements and a `CiliumLoadBalancerIPPool`. 2. `kubectl create namespace foo && kubectl create namespace foo-bar` 3. Create Service `bar-baz` of type LoadBalancer in `foo`, and Service `baz` of type LoadBalancer in `foo-bar`. 4. Create `CiliumL2AnnouncementPolicy` objects selecting both, with disjoint `nodeSelector`s so the two Services are announced from different nodes. 5. `kubectl get leases -n kube-system | grep cilium-l2announce` shows one Lease named `cilium-l2announce-foo-bar-baz` instead of two. ### Cilium Version N/A — found by source inspection, no live cluster involved. ### Kernel Version N/A — found by source inspection, no live cluster involved. ### Kubernetes Version N/A — found by source inspection, no live cluster involved. ### Regression _No response_ ### Sysdump _No response_ ### Relevant log output ```shell ``` ### Anything else? _No response_ ### Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? Please add yourself to the [Users doc](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/USERS.md) ### Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: Host datapath BPF programs leak on every device change, exhausting kernel executable memory
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.20.0 and lower than v1.21.0 ### What happened? A bonded interface on the node was being torn down and recreated every ~34s (unrelated host misconfiguration). The bond carries three VLAN sub-interfaces, so each cycle removes and re-adds three managed devices, producing two host-datapath reloads: ```bash 11:17:04 msg="Devices changed" devices="[eno1 interconnect]" 11:17:05 msg="Devices changed" devices="[public.3212 public.3211 eno1 interconnect public.1537]" 11:17:37 msg="Devices changed" devices="[eno1 interconnect]" 11:17:38 msg="Devices changed" devices="[public.1537 public.3212 public.3211 eno1 interconnect]" 11:18:11 msg="Devices changed" devices="[eno1 interconnect]" 11:18:12 msg="Devices changed" devices="[public.1537 public.3212 public.3211 eno1 interconnect]" ``` Each reload leaked a full generation of host datapath programs and their tail-call maps. After 21h uptime: ```bash $ bpftool prog show | grep -cE '^[0-9]+:' 74678 $ bpftool map show | grep -c prog_array 6034 ``` The leak is confined to the per-device path. There are 80 pods on this node, and every per-endpoint program count is exactly 80, while every per-device count is ~5950: ```bash $ bpftool prog show | awk '{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i=="name") print $(i+1)}' \ | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20 6029 tail_no_service_ipv4 <-- leaked 6029 tail_nodeport_rev_dnat_ingress_ipv4 <-- leaked 5949 tail_handle_snat_fwd_ipv4 <-- leaked 5948 tail_handle_ipv4_from_netdev <-- leaked 5948 tail_handle_ipv4_from_host <-- leaked 80 tail_ipv4_to_endpoint <-- correct, == pod count 80 tail_ipv4_ct_ingress <-- correct 80 tail_handle_arp <-- correct ``` Each leaked generation has a distinct program tag, so these are separate compilations that were never released, not multiple references to one program. Reloads frequently abort part-way, because the device disappears while the agent is working on it. Programs are already loaded into the kernel at this point: ```bash level=warn msg="Failed to initialize datapath, retrying later" module=agent.datapath.orchestrator error="failed to retrieve link public.1537 by name: Link not found" ``` ### Impact we got JIT images are allocated from the kernel executable memory region (~1520 MiB on x86_64). The leaked programs filled it: ``` $ grep -E 'bpf_jit|execmem|bpf_prog_pack' /proc/vmallocinfo \ | awk '{c=$3; sub(/\+0x.*/,"",c); s[c]+=$2; n[c]++} \ END {for (k in s) printf "%10.2f MiB %6d %s\n", s[k]/1024/1024, n[k], k}' 987.84 MiB 492 bpf_prog_pack_alloc $ dmesg | grep -c 'execmem: unable to allocate memory' 12466 # in a 2.16-hour window ``` With `CONFIG_BPF_JIT_ALWAYS_ON=y` a failed JIT allocation cannot fall back to the interpreter and returns `-ENOTSUPP` (errno 524). Seccomp filter installation is the most frequent BPF load on a Kubernetes node, so **every container exec fails**: ``` containerd: msg="ExecSync for ... failed" error="... OCI runtime exec failed: unable to init seccomp: error loading seccomp filter into kernel: error loading seccomp filter: errno 524" ``` Exec probes then fail node-wide, pods never become ready, and the node is dead. Only a reboot recovers it. Measured rate: ~3400 leaked programs/hour, so the node dies roughly **one day after every boot** while device churn continues. ### How can we reproduce the issue? On a node with Cilium device auto-detection enabled: ```bash before_p=$(bpftool prog show | grep -cE '^[0-9]+:') before_m=$(bpftool map show | grep -c prog_array) for i in $(seq 1 20); do ip link add leakparent type dummy ip link set leakparent up n=1 for v in 1537 3211 3212; do ip link add link leakparent name leakparent.$v type vlan id $v ip addr add 10.99.$n.1/24 dev leakparent.$v ip link set leakparent.$v up n=$((n+1)) done sleep 5 # let the agent start reloading ip link del leakparent # all three managed devices vanish at once, mid-reload sleep 5 done sleep 30 echo "delta: progs=$(( $(bpftool prog show | grep -cE '^[0-9]+:') - before_p ))" echo "delta: prog_arrays=$(( $(bpftool map show | grep -c prog_array) - before_m ))" ``` Expected: both deltas return to ~0. Actual: they grow monotonically and never drop. A single dummy device added and removed cleanly does **not** leak — the device must disappear while a reload is in flight. ### Cilium Version Client: 1.17.18 Daemon: 1.17.18 Updated new found at: Client: 1.20.0 450c5314 2026-07-29T08:53:01+02:00 go version go1.26.5 linux/amd64 Daemon: 1.20.0 450c5314 2026-07-29T08:53:01+02:00 go version go1.26.5 linux/amd64 ### Kernel Version 6.12.92; 7.0.0-22-generic Both by default: CONFIG_BPF_JIT_ALWAYS_ON=y ### Kubernetes Version 1.33 ### Regression _No response_ ### Sysdump From latest cilium 1.20 test: [cilium-sysdump-20260805-141731.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30748085/cilium-sysdump-20260805-141731.zip) ### Relevant log output ```shell ``` ### Anything else? Related, but both are about *agent restarts* rather than device changes: #46065, #44194. The error reported when the executable memory region is exhausted is misleading and cost us significant debugging time. The agent presents `-ENOTSUPP` as a verifier rejection and prints a stack depth: ``` Verifier error: program tail_handle_snat_fwd_ipv4: load program: operation not supported: stack depth 272 ``` Nothing is wrong with the program or its stack usage. Distinguishing `ENOTSUPP` from an actual verifier rejection would help a lot. ### Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? The `net.IPNet` half is there because `wgtypes.PeerConfig.AllowedIPs` is a `[]net.IPNet`, so the package was carrying the wgctrl representation through its own state rather than converting at the edge. This turns the three maps into sets keyed by `netip.Prefix` and moves the `net.IPNet` conversion out to the two spots that talk to wgctrl. A few other things follow from that: - `ipnetToPrefix()` called `netipx.MustFromStdIP()`, which panics if the IP is not 4 or 16 bytes. The replacement uses `netipx.FromStdIP()` and callers skip the prefix if the conversion fails. - Four blocks were building a `/32` or `/128` by hand with `net.CIDRMask()` plus an IPv4/IPv6 branch. `netip.Addr.BitLen()` already gives the right width, so those become one helper call each. Left alone on purpose: `peerConfig.nodeIPv4`/`nodeIPv6` are still `net.IP`. Converting them touches ~100 more sites in the tests and would bury this change. The `fakeWgClient` helpers and the `wgtypes.PeerConfig` literals in `cell_test.go` also stay on `net.IPNet`, since that is the API they are standing in for.
