signal.title: CFP: Network Quality of Service (QOS) API
signal.text: ## Cilium Feature Proposal **Is your proposed feature related to a problem?** Yes. Currently, Cilium's QoS implementation using bandwidth manager is a node-local solution (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/24194). It uses an internal priority field in the kernel (skb->priority) to order packets on the node, but this priority is not preserved in the packet header when it leaves the node. This means that downstream network devices like routers and switches are unaware of the packet's priority, and cannot provide end-to-end Quality of Service. **Describe the feature you'd like** We would like a declarative, Kubernetes-native way to apply QOS tagging to egress traffic from pods. This would allow administrators to define QoS policies that are respected across the entire network. **Declarative and Extensible API:** - The API must be Kubernetes-native and declarative. - It should be designed as a generic QoS framework that can be extended in the future to support mechanisms beyond DSCP, such as bandwidth shaping or other traffic control features. **Flexible Traffic Selection:** The mechanism for applying QoS policies must be flexible and support selection based on: - Workload: Kubernetes-native selectors for pods and namespaces (podSelector, namespaceSelector). - L4 Flow: Granular selection based on protocol (TCP/UDP), source port, and destination port. **Initial Use Case:** The initial implementation within this framework can focus on specific DSCP marking of egress packets. The system must allow specifying any DSCP value within the standard 0-63 range. The division and quantization of this range should be determined by Cluster Administrators, recognizing that many organizations operate complex network environments with established QoS policies that leverage the entire 0-63 DSCP range. Integration with Existing Features: - The new QoS framework should integrate with Cilium's existing features, such as the bandwidth manager and the current local traffic shaping implementation. https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/24194 **Notify relevant community channels** - @cilium/bandwidth-manager **(Optional) Describe your proposed solution** This solution outlines a persona-based approach to Quality of Service (QoS) in Cilium, designed to provide a flexible and powerful way to manage network traffic prioritization. This model introduces a clear separation of concerns by defining three distinct personas, each with specific roles and responsibilities: Cluster Providers, Infrastructure Admins, and Application Developers. **The Personas** - Cluster Providers: Define the available QoS mechanisms (e.g., DSCP, NodePriority) using the QoSMechanism CRD. - Infrastructure Admins: Create reusable QoS profiles (e.g., "low-latency", "voice", "guaranteed") from the available mechanisms using the QoSClass CRD. - Application Developers: Apply the predefined QoS classes to their workloads using the QoSPolicy CRD. **Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)** The following example shows how DSCP as well as node priority can be defined and used under the new proposed model. Node priority refers to [CFP 24194](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/24194) **QoSMechanism (Cluster Provider)** Declares a supported QoS mechanism in the cluster. ```yaml # Declares that DSCP tagging is available. apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1 kind: QoSMechanism metadata: name: dscp spec: type: DSCP description: "Provides DSCP tagging for egress traffic." --- # Declares that NodePriority (node-local FQ scheduler prioritization) is available. apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1 kind: QoSMechanism metadata: name: node-priority spec: type: NodePriority description: "Provides node-local packet prioritization using FQ scheduler priority levels." ``` **QoSClass (Infrastructure Admin)** Defines a reusable QoS profile based on an available mechanism. ```yaml # Defines a "voice" class using the dscp mechanism. apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1 kind: QoSClass metadata: name: voice spec: priority: 100 # Higher number indicates higher precedence during policy collisions mechanismRef: name: dscp parameters: value: 46 # Expedited Forwarding (EF) --- # Defines a "guaranteed" class using the node-priority mechanism. Priority is strictly mechanism-local; it resolves conflicts only between classes sharing the same underlying mechanism (e.g., DSCP vs DSCP) and does not affect orthogonal mechanisms applied concurrently. apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1 kind: QoSClass metadata: name: guaranteed spec: priority: 90 mechanismRef: name: node-priority parameters: priority: Guaranteed ``` **QoSPolicy (Application Developer)** Applies one or more QoS classes to selected pods and egress traffic flows. ```yaml # Applies the "voice" DSCP QoS class and the "guaranteed" node-priority QoS class # to egress traffic destined for 192.168.1.0/24 on UDP port 5060 and TCP port 8080. apiVersion: cilium.io/v1alpha1 kind: QoSPolicy metadata: name: payment-app-qos namespace: production spec: podSelector: matchLabels: app: payment-processor egress: - toCIDR: - 192.168.1.0/24 toPorts: - ports: - port: "5060" protocol: UDP - port: "8080" protocol: TCP qosClassRefs: - name: voice - name: guaranteed ``` ### Policy Collisions and Conflict Resolution When multiple `QoSPolicy` resources match the same pod and traffic flow, conflicts can arise if they assign different QoS classes for the same mechanism. Because mechanisms like DSCP do not have an inherent SLA hierarchy, conflicts are resolved using the following rules: - **Rule Specificity:** Granular L4 flow rules override broader L3 rules, and rules matching a more specific destination CIDR take precedence over broader CIDR matches. - **Class Priority Precedence:** When two independent policies have the exact same specificity but configure conflicting QoS classes for the same mechanism, Cilium evaluates the explicit `spec.priority` field defined on the `QoSClass` resources.

I am using Cilium Gateway API with an external Envoy DaemonSet and a hostNetwork Gateway listener. The Gateway is restricted to one node (`node B`) using: ```yaml gatewayAPI: enabled: true hostNetwork: enabled: true nodes: matchLabels: gateway-node: "true" ``` The backend Service has two healthy pod endpoints: 10.244.4.70:5556 on the same node as the Gateway/Envoy (node B) 10.244.0.92:5556 on another node (node A) Requests through the Gateway intermittently return HTTP 503: ``` upstream connect error or disconnect/reset before headers. reset reason: connection timeout ``` Envoy's cluster statistics show that the remote-node backend works consistently, while the same-node backend cannot establish a TCP connection: ``` 10.244.0.92:5556 (remote node) cx_connect_fail: 0 rq_success: >0 10.244.4.70:5556 (same node) cx_connect_fail: increasing rq_success: 0 ``` Envoy EDS contains both endpoints and marks both as healthy. signal.title: Gateway API: Envoy upstream replies from same-node backends lost (RST), nondeterministic across restarts on ARM64
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [X] I have searched the existing issues Closest matches are #47400 / #46260 / #26584, but those are about **ingress** traffic to L7LB frontends being dropped at TC on specific device types. This issue is different: ingress reaches Envoy fine — it is Envoy's **upstream replies from same-node backends** that are lost, and it is nondeterministic across agent restarts/node reboots. ### Version Reproduced on **v1.19.6** and **v1.20.0** (identical behavior). ### What happened? With Gateway API enabled, a `Gateway` + `HTTPRoute` pointing at a Deployment whose 2 replicas are spread across 2 nodes: requests through the gateway (ClusterIP or NodePort, from host netns or external clients) **alternate 200/503**. The failing half are the requests where per-request load balancing picks the backend pod on the **same node as the serving Envoy**; remote-node backends always work. Hubble for a failing request (Envoy upstream connection to the local backend): ``` 10.244.0.216:52632 (ingress) -> website/website-...:3000 (ID:7959) to-endpoint FORWARDED (TCP Flags: SYN) 10.244.0.216:52632 (host) <- website/website-...:3000 (ID:7959) to-stack FORWARDED (TCP Flags: SYN, ACK) 10.244.0.216:52632 (host) -> website/website-...:3000 (ID:7959) to-endpoint FORWARDED (TCP Flags: RST) ``` The backend's SYN-ACK goes `to-stack` **without the proxy mark**, the kernel finds no ordinary socket for the transparent-bound tuple and answers RST. `cilium-dbg monitor --type drop` shows nothing for these flows. Control-plane state is consistent the whole time: - `cilium-dbg shell -- db/show services` → `ProxyRedirect=<port> (ports: [80])` present - `cilium-dbg shell -- db/show envoy-resources` → all `Done`, no errors - `cilium-dbg service list` → ClusterIP shows `1 => 127.0.0.1:<proxyPort>/TCP (active)` - `CILIUM_PRE_mangle` TPROXY rule matches the current proxy port - Identical behavior with `bpf.tproxy=true` and `false` **Nondeterminism:** after certain agent restarts the same configuration served 8/8 *including* local backends for a few hours, then regressed to alternating after subsequent node reboots with zero config change. Health appears to depend on datapath programming order, suggesting a race. ### Eliminated during bisection - Gateway API CRD skew — fails with correctly pinned v1.3.0 (on 1.19.6) and v1.6.1 (on 1.20.0) - Kernel version skew — both nodes aligned to the same kernel build, no change - `devices` contents — fails with `{eth0,wlan0}` and `{eth0}` (transient improvement after the change, regressed after reboots) - `bpf.masquerade` true/false (iptables masquerade), `bpf.tproxy` true/false - AppArmor — zero denials involving cilium/envoy in kernel logs - systemd `MACAddressPolicy=persistent` — override to `none` for veth/vxlan applied, no change - Full `helm uninstall` + reinstall, plus clean reboots of both nodes (fresh bpffs) ### Environment (affected) - 2× Raspberry Pi 5, Ubuntu 26.04, kernel `7.0.0-1010-raspi` (also `1016`, aligned — no difference), arm64 - k3s `v1.35.4+k3s1` (`--flannel-backend=none --disable-network-policy --disable-kube-proxy --disable=servicelb --disable=traefik`) - Cilium via helm: `kubeProxyReplacement=true`, `routingMode=tunnel`, `tunnelProtocol=vxlan`, `ipam.mode=kubernetes`, `devices={eth0}`, `bpf.masquerade=false`, `MTU=1450`, `gatewayAPI.enabled=true`, external Envoy DaemonSet (defaults) - Node also has a second physical NIC (`wlan0`) outside `devices`, default route via it; inter-node traffic on `eth0` (/30) ### Not reproducible on kind (same versions, same values) The identical stack on kind serves local and remote backends 12/12, which is what makes the affected environment interesting. Full comparison recipe: ```bash cat > kind.yaml << 'K' kind: Cluster apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4 networking: {disableDefaultCNI: true, kubeProxyMode: none} nodes: [{role: control-plane}, {role: worker}, {role: worker}] K kind create cluster --config kind.yaml kubectl apply --server-side -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.6.1/experimental-install.yaml helm install cilium cilium/cilium -n kube-system --version 1.20.0 \ --set kubeProxyReplacement=true --set k8sServiceHost=kind-control-plane --set k8sServicePort=6443 \ --set ipam.mode=kubernetes --set routingMode=tunnel --set tunnelProtocol=vxlan \ --set "devices={eth0}" --set bpf.masquerade=false --set bpf.tproxy=true \ --set gatewayAPI.enabled=true --set l2announcements.enabled=true --set MTU=1450 # then: Gateway (class cilium) + HTTPRoute -> Deployment pinned to worker1, Service :80 # curl the gateway ClusterIP from worker1 (local case) and worker2 (remote case): both 100% OK on kind ``` On the affected k3s/raspi cluster the same manifests yield the alternating 200/503. ### Anything else? Happy to provide a `cilium sysdump` from the affected cluster, re-run any diagnostics, or test patches — the environment is available and the failure is easy to trigger there. Also happy to try a stock-Ubuntu k3s VM to further separate the k3s axis from the raspi kernel if that helps triage. ### Code of Conduct - [X] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: policy: Fix data race on the map state identity index
signal.text: Please ensure your pull request adheres to the following guidelines: - [x] For first time contributors, read [Submitting a pull request] - [x] All code is covered by unit and/or runtime tests where feasible. - [x] All commits contain a well written commit description including a title, description and a `Fixes: #XXX` line if the commit addresses a particular GitHub issue. - [x] If your commit description contains a `Fixes: <commit-id>` tag, then please add the commit author[s] as reviewer[s] to this issue. - [x] All commits are signed off. See the section [Developer’s Certificate of Origin] - [x] Provide a title or release-note blurb suitable for the release notes. - [x] Disclose use of machine learning models (including LLMs and other generative AI) in accordance with the [Cilium AI Policy], and indicate the rating using [AI Influence Level]. Example: "This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked X." - [x] Thanks for contributing! --- cilium-agent dies with `fatal error: concurrent map iteration and map write` when an endpoint's policy is recomputed while incremental policy map changes are applied concurrently: ``` fatal error: concurrent map iteration and map write pkg/policy.newMapState pkg/policy/mapstate.go:731 pkg/policy.(*selectorPolicy).DistillPolicy pkg/policy/resolve.go:419 pkg/endpoint.(*Endpoint).regeneratePolicy pkg/endpoint/policy.go:275 ``` `DistillPolicy` deliberately runs with the endpoint unlocked so the ipcache can make progress, but it sized the new map state from the owner's *live* previous map state — `len()` on the entries map and, when the identity index (`byId`) is in use, iterating it for per-identity key counts — while `Endpoint.ApplyPolicyMapChanges` mutates those same maps under the endpoint lock. No lock is shared between the two. This became reachable on most endpoints under ordinary pod churn when the identity-index gate was widened from pass rules to named-port rules (d1c81b3a5624); before that it needed the rarely used pass rules. ### The fix, and why the interface changes shape `PolicyOwner.PreviousMapState() *MapState` becomes `PreviousMapStateSizes() MapStateSizes`, a value snapshot taken under the endpoint lock. The pointer-returning form was not a content-access contract. Before 1c4121caba5a the interface method was `MapStateSize() int` — a pure sizing hint. That commit widened it to the whole pointer only because the new `byId` index also needed per-identity keyset sizes, and the only consumer (`newMapState`, via `resolve.go`) has ever read just lengths from it: `len(old.entries)`, `len(old.byId)` and `len(v)` per keyset. One existing mock even returns nil. This restores the original sizing-accessor contract, generalized to carry the per-identity sizes the index needs, with the snapshot taken under the right lock. The accessor is called before the selector cache read lock is taken: the endpoint takes the selector cache write lock while holding its own lock (e.g. when `setDesiredPolicy` detaches a superseded policy), so taking the endpoint lock inside `WithRLock` would invert the established lock order and deadlock. Cost of the snapshot is O(#identities in the index): ~+175µs, +148KB, +18 allocs per `DistillPolicy` at a worst-case 4096-identity index, noise otherwise — microseconds against multi-millisecond regenerations. ### Backport Suggest backporting to v1.20: both `Fixes:` commits are in v1.20, so the crash is reachable there. The commit cherry-picks cleanly onto the current v1.20 head and the touched packages pass unit, `-race`, integration and privileged suites there. ### Follow-ups, deliberately not in this PR - The same race class remains in the `cilium-dbg policy` commands, which read live map state unlocked after `GetDesiredPolicy` returns: `pkg/policy/commands/topk.go:130` and `pkg/policy/commands/mapstate.go:73`. - The `rlockAlive`-error branch of the new accessor (disconnecting endpoint → zero sizes) has no dedicated test; a one-line companion test can follow. - Pre-existing breakage on main, unrelated but hit while validating: `TestComputeCIDRLabels` flakes under `-race` (leaked controller goroutine from `TestInitialNamedPortsIdentityLabel`); `BenchmarkRegenerateCIDRPolicyRules` (stale entry-count assert) and `BenchmarkEvaluateL4PolicyMapState/IncrementalToMapState` (index panic) both fail under `-bench`, which nothing in CI runs. Adding @jrajahalme as reviewer, as the author of both `Fixes:` commits. This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked the diff, the lock-order reasoning against the selector-cache and endpoint lock paths, the regression tests and their mutation checks, and the validation results below. Validation: five regression tests (race detector plus a deadlock watchdog), each mutation-checked; containerised unit, integration and privileged suites with no failures attributable to this branch; and a live cluster running a `-race` + go-deadlock agent image through ~2h of pod and policy churn with named-port policies active, with zero race, deadlock or crash reports. ```release-note Fixed a cilium-agent crash (`fatal error: concurrent map iteration and map write`) when an endpoint's policy was recomputed while incremental policy map changes were being applied concurrently. This was most commonly triggered by policies using named ports under pod churn. ``` [AI Influence Level]: https://danielmiessler.com/blog/ai-influence-level-ail [Cilium AI Policy]: https://github.com/cilium/community/blob/main/AI-POLICY.md [Developer’s Certificate of Origin]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#dev-coo [Submitting a pull request]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#submitting-a-pull-request

signal.title: CFP: Support dynamic IP address allocation in Cilium Network Driver
signal.text: ### Is your proposed feature related to a problem? The Cilium Network Driver proposed in [cilium/cilium#43295](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/43295) and [CFP-43295](https://github.com/cilium/design-cfps/pull/85) can allocate and prepare network devices for Pods through Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA). Those devices may also need IPv4 and/or IPv6 addresses, but the Network Driver does not have a scalable way to allocate them dynamically. Requiring a cluster operator to assign static addresses does not scale and is particularly unsafe with reusable `ResourceClaimTemplate` objects: multiple claims created from the same template must not receive the same address. Cilium Pod IPAM modes cannot be used directly because these addresses belong to claimed network resources, not to the Pod's primary Cilium interface, and their allocation lifecycle follows DRA prepare/unprepare operations rather than CNI endpoint creation and deletion. Without dedicated resource IPAM, operators must maintain per-workload address assignments themselves, cannot safely reuse claim templates, and cannot independently manage address capacity for different secondary networks or device classes. ### Describe the feature you'd like Add dedicated IPAM support for the Cilium Network Driver. It should manage addresses for DRA network resources and coexist with any IPAM mode used for Pods; enabling it must not change or consume capacity from Pod IPAM. ### Requirements - Support IPv4-only, IPv6-only, and dual-stack configurations. Allow cluster operators to define the address spaces available to DRA resources, including efficient use of small address ranges. - Support independently managed address spaces for different secondary networks or device classes, and allow each DRA device request to identify its intended address space. Cilium must not silently allocate an address from a different network when the requested address space is unavailable. - Allocate the required address or addresses while preparing a DRA `ResourceClaim`, before the device is configured for the Pod. The allocated addresses must be exposed through the claim's allocated-device status so that the result is inspectable and can be restored. - Make claim operations idempotent. Retrying preparation must preserve the existing allocation rather than consume another address. Cilium component restarts must not change live allocations, and a partially failed preparation must roll back any newly allocated addresses. - Release addresses when the claim is unprepared and they are no longer used. Stale capacity must be reclaimed safely when nodes or claims disappear. - Handle concurrent claims without duplicate live allocations within the same address space. Missing configuration, address-family mismatches, and exhaustion must leave the claim unprepared and surface an actionable, retryable error. - Scale across large node counts and high claim churn without allocation latency or API-server and control-plane load becoming a bottleneck. Unused capacity must be reclaimable safely. - Cover the allocation, retry, restart/restore, rollback, release, exhaustion, IPv4, IPv6, and dual-stack paths with automated tests and document the operational lifecycle. ### Scope and non-goals This issue is limited to IP address management for network devices handled by the Cilium Network Driver. It does not propose changes to device discovery, DRA scheduling, SR-IOV or other device-manager behavior, VLAN or route configuration, NRI integration, or Cilium datapath connectivity for the secondary interface. It also does not replace existing Pod IPAM modes or track static address assignment. ### Notify relevant community channels @cilium/network-driver @cilium/sig-ipam

signal.title: gha/kubespray: don't wait for CoreDNS before Cilium is installed
signal.text: We run kubespray with kube_network_plugin=cni, so kubespray writes no CNI configuration and there is no pod network until Cilium is installed, yet bring-up waited for every kube-system pod to be Ready. That only worked by accident, because the old image installed podman from the Ubuntu archive and cri-dockerd picked up its /etc/cni/net.d/87-podman-bridge.conflist. The new image ships a static podman that uses netavark, leaving /etc/cni/net.d empty, so the wait can never be satisfied. Wait for the host-network control plane instead, and assert kube-system readiness after Cilium is up, where CoreDNS not converging is a real failure. Also dump cluster state on bring-up failure, since the sysdump step is skipped when Cilium was never installed. This PR was prepared with AIL:3.

signal.title: gha: bound the LLVM prereq apt step with a 5m timeout
signal.text: In run 32225900868 the "Install LLVM and Clang prerequisites" step of build-commits-test hung inside apt-get for 2h51m and only stopped because the run was cancelled by hand. The step has no bound of its own, so the only thing that would have ended it is the job's timeout-minutes: 180, which burns nearly three hours of an extra-power runner before the PR reports anything. Across the last successful Build Commits runs the step completes in 6 to 18 seconds, so 5 minutes leaves plenty of headroom for a slow mirror while still failing fast when apt wedges. A hung apt is not something a retry inside the step can recover from, so failing the job and letting it be re-run is the right outcome. This PR was prepared with AIL:3.

signal.title: operator/identitygc: remove write-only type GC fields
signal.text: These `type GC` fields are only written but never read. The respective values are already used to configure `GC.heartbeatStore` and `GC.rateLimiter`, respectively. There is no point in keeping these copies, so remove them.

signal.title: bpf: migrate non-branching config macros to runtime configuration
signal.text: The current step in the clang-freedom (pre-compiled eBPF programs) journey is to start transitioning compile time configuration to load-time (runtime) configuration. The necessary agent and loader infrastructure has been merged. Runtime configuration can be defined with [`DECLARE_CONFIG` and `NODE_CONFIG`](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/bpf/lib/static_data.h). See [Configuring the Datapath](https://docs.cilium.io/en/latest/contributing/development/datapath_config) in the Cilium Developer docs for guidelines and principles. ~~This issue specifically tracks variables which do not influence control flow by enabling or disabling certain code paths. Variables used in `#ifdef`/`#if` and `if(is_defined(...))` will be converted in 1.19 since dead code elimination only really landed in Linux 5.5, and Cilium 1.18 targets Linux 5.4 which will go EOL at the end of 2025.~~ 1.19 targets Linux 5.10. We can migrate branching macros, too. Additionally, https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/41628 shipped in 1.19 which added dead code detection in the agent to avoid loading unused maps and tail calls. Branching macros can now safely be ported. This issue is for migrating `node_config.h` and `WriteNodeConfig` entries to `config.Node`, as well as some leftover per-object configs in `ep_config.h`. Through this issue, we can coordinate work and keep an overview. If you want to work on a particular (set of) variable(s), drop a comment and we'll spin out an issue or assign you to a list item. The list may change over time and may grow as we find more work in this category. When migrating variables, do a quick search through [Paul's macro documentation](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/15379#issuecomment-897441189) for a good docstring to use in `DECLARE_CONFIG`. - [ep_config.h](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/bpf/ep_config.h) - [x] HOST_EP_ID - [x] DIRECT_ROUTING_DEV_IFINDEX - [node_config.h](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/bpf/node_config.h) - [x] CLUSTER_ID - [x] CILIUM_*_IFINDEX, CILIUM_*_MAC (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/43474) - [x] TUNNEL_PORT, TUNNEL_PROTOCOL (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/43520) - [x] KERNEL_HZ, ENABLE_JIFFIES (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/43112) - [x] L2_ANNOUNCEMENTS(_MAX_LIVENESS) (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/42587) - [x] EPHEMERAL_MIN (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/43564) - [x] IS_L3_DEV, NATIVE_DEV_MAC_BY_IFINDEX (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/39116 & https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/43680) - [x] CLUSTER_ID_MAX (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/42478) - [x] IDENTITY_{LEN,MAX} (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/43507) - [x] VTEP_MASK (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/43112) - [x] NODEPORT_PORT_* (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/43680) - [x] IPV4_LOOPBACK (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/38818) - [x] NAT_46X64_PREFIX (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/43799) - [x] CIDR_IDENTITY_RANGE_{START,END} (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44223) - [x] HASH_INIT{4,6}_SEED (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44190) - [x] EVENTS_MAP_* (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/pull/44795) - [ ] VLAN_FILTER (https://github.com/cilium/cilium/issues/38721) - [x] Reserved security IDs (HOST_ID, WORLD_ID, ect.) signal.title: fix: remove duplicate entries in values.schema.json anyOf arrays
signal.text: ## What this PR does The `values.schema.json` file contained numerous `anyOf` arrays with duplicate entries. For example: - `securityContext.capabilities.ciliumAgent.items.anyOf` had **13 identical entries** (should be 1) - `ingressController.ingressLBAnnotationPrefixes.items.anyOf` had **5 identical entries** (should be 1) - `operator.tolerations.items.anyOf` had **4 identical entries** (should be 1) This was functionally correct but confused new developers reading the schema. ## Changes - Deduplicated all `anyOf` arrays in `install/kubernetes/cilium/values.schema.json` - **1 line added, 167 lines removed** - No semantic change — the schema validates the same values as before ## Verification Ran 30 test cases comparing original and modified schemas: - ✅ All duplicates removed (38 duplicate entries → 0) - ✅ All unique entries preserved - ✅ Schema structure unchanged - ✅ File size reduced (170KB → 166KB) - ✅ Valid JSON with correct 2-space indentation Ref: #41099

signal.title: bgp: gate BGP announcements on host datapath init
signal.text: ## Description The BGP Control Plane controller starts reconciling as soon as the CiliumNode resource becomes available, which happens before `bpf_host.c` has been attached to native devices. On node reboot, this caused a "No route to host" window: the upstream router added the node back to its ECMP group, but incoming LB traffic arrived on native devices with no BPF program to DNAT it. Fix by blocking `Run()` on `Loader.HostDatapathInitialized()` before entering the event loop. The channel is closed by `ReloadDatapath()` once the host endpoint BPF programs have been attached. `Loader` is already available in the Hive dependency graph and is injected via `ControllerParams`. ## Reproduction **Setup** - Two nodes acting as BGP ECMP peers for a LoadBalancer service (`externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster`) - Upstream router distributes traffic across both nodes via ECMP - Build Cilium with a `time.Sleep(30 * time.Second)` added at the top of `ReloadDatapath()` in `pkg/datapath/loader/endpoint.go`, and deploy the modified image as the cilium-agent on both nodes **Steps to reproduce** 1. Reboot one of the two nodes 2. Send requests to the LoadBalancer VIP from an external client during the 30-second window after the rebooted node's BGP session re-establishes **Observed behavior** "No route to host" errors occur during the window. Depending on which ECMP bucket the client's 5-tuple hashes to, the failure rate should be either 100% or 0% per flow. **Expected behavior** No errors: BGP should not advertise routes until BPF programs are attached to native devices. ```release-note Fix a "No route to host" window on node reboot where BGP advertised routes before BPF programs were attached to native devices. ``` This PR was prepared with AIL:3. I personally checked the datapath attachment sequence and the HostDatapathInitialized channel lifecycle.

signal.title: Gateway API: intermittent fixed ~5.02s stall before request is proxied upstream (v1.19.4, VXLAN, no node encryption)
signal.text: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Version equal or higher than v1.19.6 and lower than v1.20.0 ### What happened? # Gateway API: intermittent fixed ~5.02s stall before request is proxied upstream (v1.19.4, VXLAN, no node encryption) ## Summary Requests through a Gateway API listener intermittently stall for a fixed **~5.02 seconds** before the request is proxied to the backend. The backend never sees the request during the stall. Envoy reports no timeouts, retries, or circuit-breaker events, and there is no 5s value anywhere in the effective Envoy config. No requests are lost — with a client timeout above 5s everything completes successfully. Reproducible across four independent clusters. Rate correlates **inversely** with node count, which we cannot explain. ## Environment - Cilium **v1.19.4**, cilium-envoy **v1.36.6** - Gateway API, `kube-proxy-replacement=true` - `routing-mode=tunnel` (VXLAN), jumbo MTU (`cilium_vxlan` 9001, `cilium_wg0` 8921, physical NIC 9001) - `enable-wireguard=true` with **`NodeEncryption: Disabled`** - Managed Kubernetes on AWS, arm64 (Graviton) nodes; Amazon Linux 2023, kernel `6.12.88-119.157.amzn2023.aarch64` - Gateway fronted by an internal L4 load balancer (instance targets, cross-zone enabled, client-IP preservation on) Relevant cilium-config values (no 5s among them): ``` proxy-connect-timeout: 2 proxy-idle-timeout-seconds: 60 http-stream-idle-timeout: 300 proxy-initial-fetch-timeout: 30 gateway-api-service-externaltrafficpolicy: Cluster ``` Effective Envoy config timeouts (from `/config_dump`): `idle_timeout 60s`, `stream_idle_timeout 300s`, `connect_timeout 2s`, `initial_fetch_timeout 30s`, plus `600s`/`900s` route timeouts. **No 5s value.** ## Symptom Client is a pod in-cluster calling an HTTPS hostname routed to the internal Gateway. `curl` timing on a stalled request: ``` total=5.024006 time_appconnect=0.023203 time_starttransfer=5.023998 code=000 ``` TLS completes normally (~23ms), then nothing for ~5.0s. The stall lands at 5.02s regardless of client timeout: | Client timeout | Result | | --- | --- | | `--max-time 5` | 28/30 | | `--max-time 20` | 28/30, the 2 slow ones at **5.025s** and **5.024s** | | `--max-time 30` | **60/60 complete**, 7 slow | Raising the client timeout does not move where the stall lands, so this is not client impatience. ## The backend never receives the request during the stall Backend has a **single replica**, so the backend node is constant and only the Envoy node varies per request. `tcpdump` in the backend pod's netns, correlated with per-request timings. For a request that stalled from `02:18:48.8` to `02:18:53.9`, the backend received **zero packets** for the whole window — the next SYN to `:8080` arrives at `02:18:53.944`, i.e. only after the stall clears: ``` 02:18:48.764381 In IP <envoy-a>.46017 > <backend>.8080: Flags [S] ... 02:18:48.802412 In IP <envoy-b>.42843 > <backend>.8080: Flags [S] ... 02:18:48.838080 In IP <envoy-a>.44405 > <backend>.8080: Flags [S] ... 02:18:48.874295 In IP <envoy-c>.32887 > <backend>.8080: Flags [S] ... ... 5 SECOND GAP, nothing to the backend ... 02:18:53.944994 In IP <envoy-d>.45869 > <backend>.8080: Flags [S] ... ``` Largest inter-packet gaps on the backend side were `5.066s` and `5.056s`, matching the stalls. Client-side capture of a stalled vs a succeeding connection — byte-identical until the request, then: | | Success | Stalled | | --- | --- | --- | | request (`len 136`) sent | `39.480903` | `39.519219` | | next activity | `39.492036` (**+11ms**) | `44.518844` (**+5000ms**) | So the request is sent and ACKed at TCP level, but not proxied upstream for ~5s. ## The backend is never slow ``` cluster...<backend>_8080.upstream_rq_time: P0=4ms P50=6.0ms P90=7.1ms P99=9.1ms P100=9.1ms ``` Max upstream request time across 90 requests: **9.1ms**. ## Envoy reports no timeout of any kind Zero on all of: `upstream_rq_timeout`, `upstream_rq_retry`, `upstream_rq_per_try_timeout`, `upstream_cx_connect_timeout`, `upstream_cx_overflow`, `circuit_breakers`. No listener `downstream_cx_overflow`, no `downstream_pre_cx_timeout`, no overload-manager activity. Counters that did move over a 60-request run with 7 stalls: | Counter | Value | | --- | --- | | `upstream_cx_idle_timeout` | 44 | | `upstream_cx_destroy_local` | 44 | | `upstream_cx_total` | 47 | | `upstream_rq_per_cx` | P50=2.0 | | `downstream_cx_delayed_close_timeout` | 2 | | `upstream_rq_pending_total` | 41 → 47 | We initially suspected upstream connection-pool churn from this, but **ruled it out**: another cluster with the *lowest* stall rate (~2%) idle-reaps **100%** of its upstream connections (e.g. 103 requests over 102 connections) versus 94% here. Higher churn, lower stall rate — so aggressive idle-reaping appears to be normal behaviour and is not the mechanism. ## Only via the Gateway | Path | Result | Stalls | | --- | --- | --- | | Internal Gateway | 28/30 at 5s timeout | 2 | | k8s Service (`http://svc:8080`) | **30/30** | **0** | | Direct pod IP | **20/20** | **0** | ## Rates across four clusters (5s client timeout, so these are stall rates) | Cluster | Relative node count | Internal Gateway | External Gateway | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | A | largest (~4.5x smallest) | ~2% | 0% | | B | ~2.2x smallest | ~6% | 0% | | C | smallest | ~18% | 0% | | D | smallest | ~11% | 0% | Cilium version, cilium-envoy version, cilium-config, Gateway API config, load-balancer and target-group attributes, Envoy coverage, MTU, and pod/service CIDRs are identical across all four. **External** Gateway listeners in the same clusters are unaffected (0%). The inverse correlation with node count is consistent but unexplained. It is not a bad AZ or a bad LB node — pinning each load-balancer IP individually gives a uniform rate (2, 3, 2 stalls out of 25 each). ## Ruled out (with evidence) load-balancer target health · Gateway API config · load-balancer/target-group attributes · BPF rate limiting · connection reuse and idle timeout · ALPN · cilium datapath drops (`cilium-dbg monitor --type drop` captured 0 during a live failure) · Hubble drops · Envoy `no_filter_chain_match` · Envoy protocol errors · listen-queue overflow · node churn/age · Envoy coverage · cilium version/config differences · WireGuard · MTU · CIDR collision · client DNS (`time_namelookup` is 1.5ms on stalled requests; `ndots:5` search-path expansion investigated and excluded) · `wireguard-persistent-keepalive=0s` (stalls persist under continuous back-to-back load, including consecutive stalls) · upstream connection-pool churn (see above) · TCP RSTs observed in-pod (they appear on successful requests too — ordinary client teardown) ## Notes on related issues - #40428 (v1.18 hardcoded 5s `connectTimeout`) — fix shipped in v1.19.0; we are on v1.19.4 and our `connect_timeout` is `2s`, so this is not it. - #32592 — we already run `encryption.enabled: true` + `encryption.type: wireguard`, the workaround reported there, and still stall. That report is hostNetwork + VPC-CNI chaining with 100% cross-node failure; ours is intermittent, no hostNetwork. - #46100 — enabling `encryption.nodeEncryption: true` on one cluster took our stall rate from ~12% to **100%**, matching #46100's conditions (VXLAN + node encryption, NIC MTU 9000, `wg0` 8921, v1.19.3+). We reverted. Note this is a **separate** problem: with node encryption disabled we see **no fragmentation drops at all** (`cilium_ipv4_frag_datagrams` untouched, no `DROP_FRAG_NOT_FOUND`), yet the ~12% stall persists. ## What would help Any pointer to what, in the Gateway API path, could defer proxying an already-accepted request by a fixed ~5s without incrementing any Envoy timeout counter. We are happy to run further captures or provide a sysdump. ### How can we reproduce the issue? ## Reproduction / methods used Packet capture inside a pod (streaming via `kubectl debug -it` was unreliable for us; write to a file and read via `kubectl logs`): ```bash kubectl -n <ns> debug <pod> --image=nicolaka/netshoot:latest --target=<container> -q -- \ bash -c 'tcpdump -i any -nn -S -tttt "tcp port 443" > /tmp/c.txt & sleep 3; <drive traffic>; kill -INT %1; <analyse>' kubectl -n <ns> logs <pod> -c <debugger-name> ``` Envoy admin stats from a node (no curl in the envoy/agent images): ```bash curl -s --unix-socket /var/run/cilium/envoy/sockets/admin.sock http://localhost/stats ``` The Envoy listener port for a Gateway changes on reconfiguration — read it from `/listeners` rather than hardcoding. ### Cilium Version **Environment** - Cilium `v1.19.4`, cilium-envoy `v1.36.6` - `routing-mode=tunnel` (VXLAN), `kube-proxy-replacement=true` - Managed Kubernetes on AWS, **arm64** (Graviton) nodes - Jumbo frames: physical NIC `9001`, `cilium_vxlan` `9001`, `cilium_wg0` **`8921`** ### Kernel Version - Amazon Linux 2023, kernel `6.12.88-119.157.amzn2023.aarch64` ### Kubernetes Version - Managed Kubernetes 1.35 on AWS, **arm64** (Graviton) nodes ### Regression _No response_ ### Sysdump _No response_ ### Relevant log output ```shell ``` ### Anything else? _No response_ ### Cilium Users Document - [ ] Are you a user of Cilium? Please add yourself to the [Users doc](https://github.com/cilium/cilium/blob/main/USERS.md) ### Code of Conduct - [x] I agree to follow this project's Code of Conduct

signal.title: bpf: dsr: fix outer SrcIP in ICMP error msg
signal.text: By the time that we check whether a DSR request exceeds the MTU (and respond with an ICMP error msg), the request has already been DNATed to the backend IP/port (when using "opt" or "geneve" dispatch). We are currently RevNATing only the inner headers (the original request) - but the outer IP header still uses the backend's IP as sourceIP. Instead of fixing this up manually, split the code into two stages 1. RevNAT of the rejected DSR request, and then 2. use generate_icmp*_reply() to produce the ICMP msg, replacing all the custom rewrite logic. Note that for IPIP the request is in its original form at this point, and doesn't require any RevNAT processing. ```release-note When using DSR with --bpf-lb-dsr-dispatch set to "opt" or "geneve" in combination with --enable-pmtu-discovery, fix the outer source IP of the ICMP error message which is generated when a forwarded DSR request exceeds the network interface's MTU. ```

signal.title: datapath/l2responder: use l3 socket for v6 solicited node responder
signal.text: the l2 responder allows cilium to respond for non local ips (ex: service VIPs) by opening a l2 socket over the iface, which in turn programs the nic filtering to let ipv6 solicited node requests to be passed up the stack. this works well under the assumption that the solicited node multicasts are always flooded, but in case of an upstream switch that does MLD snooping, traffic is not flooded unless the node explicitly joins the group. this commit changes the layer2 socket approach with a l3 socket approach, so MLD joins are sent out whenever the agent needs to respond for a particular address. Fixes: #46274 ```release-note datapath/l2responder: use l3 sockets for solicited node multicast signaling ``` [AI Influence Level]: https://danielmiessler.com/blog/ai-influence-level-ail AIL 2 [Cilium AI Policy]: https://github.com/cilium/community/blob/main/AI-POLICY.md [Developer’s Certificate of Origin]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#dev-coo [Submitting a pull request]: https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/contributing/development/contributing_guide/#submitting-a-pull-request
